Sports.title: Video: Honda explain Zandvoort ‘spec 2’ power unit changes | Brief
Sports.content:
Honda will introduce a ‘spec 2’ version of its RA626H power unit at the Dutch Grand Prix. The Japanese manufacturer is racing to catch up with its rivals after experiencing serious problems with vibration and insufficient power at the start of the sesason.

General trackside manager Shintaro Orihara said the new specification had hit their internal targets. “We focused to improve engine performance to make combustion faster,” he explained in a video released by Honda.

“We changed pre-chamber to make the combustion faster, and also we changed the piston shape also to get good combustion. Also, we modified some of the lubrication system to reduce friction. So we had a quite big risk to improve engine performance.”

Sports.title: Verstappen vs Hadjar: 2026 F1 team mates’ head-to-head scores at summer break | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar began his first full season at Red Bull knowing that the last driver in the same position as him lasted just two rounds before being booted out.

That must have been a daunting prospect to contemplate, though it bears pointing out that the senior race team management has changed significantly at Red Bull since Liam Lawson was shown the door after his pair of starts for the team last year.

The more experienced Yuki Tsunoda took Lawson’s place and became the latest in a series of drivers whose reputations took a brutal battering from occupying the garage adjacent to Max Verstappen’s. Tsunoda mustered just 7.2% of Red Bull’s points while alongside Verstappen.

This is the context in which to assess Hadjar’s performance this year. His 8-2 deficit in qualifying is nothing to brag about but he has been much closer to Verstappen over a single flying lap than his predecessors.

Hadjar has done vastly better at collecting points, too, claiming 38% of Red Bull’s score so far. True, compared to Tsunoda he’s had the benefit of a wider field spread between Red Bull and the midfield, but even so he’s already taken more than twice as many points as Tsunoda managed over his 22-race stint at the team last year.

He has achieved this alongside a formidable talent in a car which both drivers have termed “undriveable” on occasions. While the high level Verstappen operates at is so familiar it can almost be taken for granted (his superb second place in Hungary, for example), Hadjar has done a more than respectable job alongside him so far.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Has F1 failed to promote quality racing? | Brief
Sports.content:
Those in charge of Formula 1 have allowed its new rules to turn racing into a ‘battle of the bots’, says @RedPill:

I felt there was going to be some trust and proper direction within FIA and Liberty Media who owns the rights to F1 to make sure the quality of (human) racing was going to remain high quality. Boy, we were wrong. The whole debacle and agreed verbiage in contacts allowed the power unit manufacturers and investors to pretty much be the ones to dictate what was going to be allowed in F1, while retaining huge powers in the wording to prevent changes.

Fans, drivers, teams, FIA and Liberty Media are now stuck with it. I hate how the drivers are more passengers in their own cars while racing. Yes, there’s too much going in the cars, that the drivers can’t possibly manage everything and race in full anger, but this is no secret or anything new. The powers that be needed to craft specifications that used the latest tech, but still retain the drivers’ ability to fully race the car, the way a race car driver is suppose to race. That is why we watch the races.

We come and watch these F1 races because there’s humans in control of brilliant machinery, racing them to the ninth degree, but there’s a limit. If I wanted to watch automated machinery duke it out and see battle of bots I would instead go to robot contests, not F1.

Red Pill (@RedPill)

Sports.title: Which of Antonelli’s rivals is his biggest threat for the championship this year? | Debates and Polls
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli’s strong position in the lead of the championship standings at the summer break is remarkable enough already for a driver in his second season in Formula 1.

But what makes his position all the more impressive is that, arguably, no single driver has yet emerged as his clear rival. Antonelli has won six of the 11 rounds so far, more than the rest put together, and only his team mate George Russell has taken multiple wins.

Despite that, Russell is not Antonelli’s closest rival in the standings: Lewis Hamilton is leading a resurgent Ferrari. Plus, the final round before the summer break saw McLaren claim their first victory of the season. Three of the last five grands prix were won by teams other than Mercedes – could Antonelli biggest threat come from one of them?

Lewis Hamilton

50 points behind

The possibility of Hamilton fighting for the championship against the driver who took the Mercedes seat he vacated last year is a compelling narrative. But is it a likely outcome? Hamilton is Antonelli’s closest rival in the points but has missed opportunities due to penalties in recent races.

George Russell

59 points behind

Russell should be Antonelli’s closest rival for the championship but various factors have left him well behind including unreliability (not that Antonelli has been immune), some misfortune and his risky first-lap lunge at Spa. He’s also on course to incur a power unit change penalty before his team mate. Still, Russell should have the equipment and the experience to put Antonelli under pressure.

Charles Leclerc

81 points behind

Hamilton may be closer to Antonelli in the standings but Charles Leclerc has arguably looked more competitive. Providing he avoids a repeat of the dip he fell into around Spain and Monaco, he could emerge as Antonelli’s biggest threat.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Lando Norris

91 points behind

Like Mercedes, unreliability has dogged McLaren this year. They often haven’t been quick enough either, though Norris has now won both a grand prix and a sprint race. The MCL40’s Hungaroring upgrade clearly paid off, and may prove enough to bring the McLarens into regular contention. The reigning world champion is a long way behind, though.

Max Verstappen

110 points behind

If last year demonstrated anything, it is unwise to write off Max Verstappen if he is not mathematically out of contention. Having been 104 points off the lead with 249 remaining, he eventually lost by the narrowest margin in F1 history (relatively). But lying 110 points behind in a car which hasn’t won a grand prix yet may be too much even for him.

Oscar Piastri

127 points behind

Oscar Piastri has proved a close match on pace for his team mate as usual but he’s even further behind in the standings. He went into the final round of last season with a shot at the championship but that doesn’t look likely to happen this year.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Isack Hadjar

151 points behind

Isack Hadjar has impressed with the quality of his performances alongside Verstappen and may yet recover the points he dropped after losing his podium finish in Monaco. But his points deficit to Antonelli is surely too large and the Red Bull not competitive enough yet for him to be a realistic title contender.

I say

Hamilton may be closest in the points but Russell surely has the better combination of opportunity and equipment at the moment. If he can stop the rot in the second half of the season I would back him to put Antonelli under pressure for the title.

Sports.title: Can Kaye Scott Pull Off The Massive Upset Against Claressa Shields?
Sports.content:
A product of Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, Kaye Scott had a decorated 15-year amateur career on the Australian national team. Scott made her pro debut in November 2023 as she outpointed Connie Chan.

In the second fight of her pro career, Kaye Scott defeated Desley Robinson via majority decision. Nine months later, Scott and Robinson would participate in a high-stakes rematch.

Much like the first fight, Kaye Scott came out very aggressively, as she pressed forward and worked off the jab. It was a very competitive, action-packed bout, but in the end, Desley Robinson defeated Scott and won the vacant IBF middleweight world title.

One year later, Kaye Scott would receive another chance to fight for a world title. This time she took advantage of the opportunity as she beat Olivia Curry via majority decision and won the WBC and vacant WBA titles.

Now the 42-year-old Kaye Scott (5-1-1) is set to face the biggest challenge of her professional career. On the night of August 15th, Scott will be defending her unified title against a woman who is a 19-time world champion.

Kaye Scott is a pressure fighter who’s most effective in the mid-range. Her opponent, Claressa Shields, is a technical boxer who has all the tools. Shields has the high IQ, footwork, elite handspeed, and excellent punch placement.

Realistically speaking, most fight fans feel Scott is overmatched, and it should be a short night of work for Shields. However, there are two distinct reasons why the defending champion has a chance to pull off the upset of the year.

The first reason is the fact that Scott is familiar with Shields because she is a former sparring partner. The second reason is due to the weight cut. In her last ring appearance, Shields fought at 173.6 pounds.

In the upcoming unified middleweight world title fight, Claressa Shields has to drop down to 160. Shields has been competing at heavyweight for the past two years, and the question is, will the weight cut affect her power and stamina?

Kaye Scott hasn’t been doing much talking, but in a recent IG post, the defending WBC, WBA middleweight world champion displayed confidence.

“Locked in for August 15th. No noise. No distractions. Stay in my lane, and bring the heat.”

Sports.title: Dmitry Bivol Facing August 20 WBO Deadline For Callum Smith Defense
Sports.content:
Olivieri stated that the extension through August 20 fits the WBO policy of maintaining one world champion per division while eliminating interim belts.

The order puts pressure on Bivol, who holds the WBO title along with the IBF and IBO belts. Callum holds the WBO interim title and has been waiting for his shot at the full championship.

Both fighters work with Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom, which should simplify negotiations compared to promotional rivalries.

Bivol returned from elbow surgery on May 30, defeating Michael Eifert by a 12-round wide unanimous decision in Ekaterinburg, Russia. All three judges scored the fight 120-107.

Smith earned his spot by defeating Joshua Buatsi by unanimous decision in February 2025. That victory gave the former super middleweight champion the WBO interim light heavyweight belt and positioned him for Bivol.

Bivol has a bigger financial option elsewhere. A third fight with Artur Beterbiev offers a far larger purse after they split their first two meetings, leaving the Smith mandatory competing with a much more lucrative fight. That leaves Bivol with nine days to decide how he handles Smith’s challenge.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Roasts BoMac Over Conor Benn Pick
Sports.content:
“Ryan is burnt. He hasn’t been the same since his first fight with Tank. He got popped. He never got back into his type,” McIntyre said to Brian Custer on his channel. “I’ve seen Benn firsthand. Man, he’s going to hurt that dude.”

The Ring amplified the knockout pick on X earlier today, drawing a response from Ryan.

“All he needs to worry about is to stop eating all them f*****g chips and taking care of his body and temple. Cause his Brain ain’t working for shit,” Garcia posted.

McIntyre left “popped” undefined, though fans familiar with Ryan’s positive Ostarine tests after his April 2024 fight against Devin Haney may connect the comment to that episode.

The Haney performance complicates the claim of a post-Tank decline. Ryan dropped Haney three times, winning a 12-round majority decision before the result was changed to a no-contest over the positive tests.

His ring return after serving the suspension offered a stronger argument for McIntyre. Garcia hit the canvas in round two against Rolly Romero in May 2025 and struggled to produce sustained offense in a unanimous decision loss.

That performance gave BoMac more ammunition for his criticism. Garcia chose personal insults rather than answering it.

Sports.title: Hearn: Devin Haney Wants Purse Without Promotional Risk
Sports.content:
“The reality is a lot of these fighters have this sort of grand illusion that they really can run their own promotional company and take over,” Hearn told the Punch Podcast. “They love to have a promotional company, and they love their logo on the ring mat and on the poster, but I’ve worked with these guys before, Devin Haney included, and when it comes down to it, they don’t really want to take any responsibility or financial risk in a show.”

Hearn gave an example involving Haney, claiming he offered a true co-promotional partnership that was quickly turned down.

“I’ve said to Devin before, you know, if you want, we’ll go 50/50 on the show. Oh, no, no, no. I said, but if it don’t work, are you going to pay half? No. Just what’s my purse?”

A true 50-50 arrangement would require sharing the financial downside if an event failed to generate enough revenue.

“You want David Diamante to go, ‘In association with Devin Haney Promotions,’” Hearn continued.

While Haney now enjoys greater control over his career decisions, Hearn maintains that independent fighters still depend on established promoters to execute major events. He pointed to Rolando Romero’s fight against Teofimo Lopez as a PBC operation, despite the fighters maintaining their own business banners.

“These guys don’t have the infrastructure and the ability to run high-level operations and shows,” Hearn said.

While maintaining a promotional entity gives Haney leverage at the negotiating table, Hearn’s point remains simple: putting your logo on a poster is vastly different from putting your own money on the line.

Sports.title: Guido Vianello Added To Thin Itauma-Hrgovic PPV
Sports.content:
The 14-3-1 contender is coming off a fifth-round knockout of Alexis Barriere last October. His recent opposition includes Richard Torrez Jr., Arslanbek Makhmudov and Efe Ajagba.

An eighth-round stoppage of Makhmudov in August 2024 is the best result on his record, coming four months after a close split decision loss to Ajagba. Torrez later defeated him by unanimous decision last April.

That experience gives the PPV another recognizable heavyweight on a card built around an intriguing but still unproven 21-year-old headliner.

Itauma is taking a major step up against 34-year-old Hrgovic for the vacant IBF heavyweight title. Hrgovic remains one of the division’s established contenders, but the punishment he has absorbed in recent fights has begun to show. Itauma is being given the opportunity to capitalize against a warhorse who may no longer be at his best.

Sam Noakes against 38-year-old former WBO lightweight champion Denys Berinchyk is the other recognizable supporting fight. Cruiserweight prospect Aloys Youmbi faces 40-year-old Mike Perez, while Constantin Ursu meets Ben Vaughan for the British and Commonwealth welterweight titles.

Beyond those bouts, the card relies largely on prospects and domestic-level fighters.

David Adeleye had previously been linked with Vianello before leaving Queensberry Promotions. With Vianello now confirmed for August 29, the quality of the opponent Queensberry finds for him becomes important on a PPV card that needs another meaningful fight.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Insists He Wants Devin Haney Fight, Hears Nothing
Sports.content:
“Haney is ducking me,” Paro told Fox Sports Australia. “I’ve said I’m good to fight by the end of October, and we ain’t heard a thing.”

Paro also rejected the idea that his financial demands caused negotiations to stall.

“I’ll fight him next, no worries. You know I’ll fight anyone. And I’ve proved that my whole career. I’ll fight him in his backyard or mine.”

The former IBF champion may have more to offer Haney commercially than Catterall. Paro brings name recognition and interest from the Australian market. Despite his loss to Richardson Hitchins, he remains a rugged southpaw with enough power and physical strength to make Haney work.

Catterall involves a different type of difficulty. He is a defensive southpaw who moves, potshots, pulls away when opponents close distance, and frequently ties up. That could produce a difficult tactical contest for Haney without necessarily generating the same financial upside as facing Paro.

Catterall’s willingness to step in still gives Haney an important bargaining chip. His manager, Sam Jones, says they have accepted the proposed date and location while accusing Paro of wanting too much money.

Haney also received some unwelcome news from Ryan Garcia this week. Garcia placed Teofimo Lopez, Rolando Romero, and Shakur Stevenson among the opponents he wants after facing Conor Benn on September 12.

“I’m not in a rush to make that fight happen,” Ryan told The Ring about facing Haney again. “They have to sit with that loss.”

That leaves Haney needing someone to fight. Paro may think the silence means Haney is avoiding him, but it may simply be Team Haney waiting to see which welterweight gives them the better deal.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma Talks Like Heavyweight’s Old Guard At 21
Sports.content:
“I like Leo Atang. He’s very decent, and he’s a nice kid as well,” Itauma told DAZN News. “I like Adam Olayinan, the guy who’s just signed with Queensberry. I watched his fight the other day, and that was very good as well. “Obviously that Teremoana, he looks decent. They’re probably the ones I’m looking at for the young guns coming up. They all look decent.”

Teremoana is about to turn 29, competed in the Olympics, and trails Itauma by only three professional bouts. Calling him one of the “young guns coming up” seems odd coming from a fighter eight years his junior.

The difference is that Itauma has been pushed much faster and surrounded by considerably more hype. Wins over Dillian Whyte, Demsey McKean, Jermaine Franklin, and Mariusz Wach have helped move him up the heavyweight rankings and create the impression that he has already graduated beyond prospect status.

Those names look better on a record than the opponents the Australian Olympian has faced, but Teremoana hasn’t been given the same type of matchmaking. He has the size and punching power to potentially run through that same tier of fighters.

Itauma gets his opportunity to show how good he really is when he faces Filip Hrgovic on August 29. Hrgovic is a significant step up from the opposition Itauma has been beating and should give a better indication of where he belongs in the division.

Until then, it’s a bit early for a 21-year-old with only three more professional fights than Teremoana to talk like an established heavyweight watching the up-and-comers work their way toward him.

Sports.title: Jerry Quarry Destroys Earnie Shavers in 141 Seconds
Sports.content:
Both fighters were 28. Quarry weighed 202 pounds, eight lighter than Shavers.

The buildup had almost guaranteed violence. Quarry predicted three rounds and believed he could finish Shavers in one if his opponent came after him. Don King, then part of Shavers’ management team, called it their easiest fight. Madison Square Garden matchmaker Teddy Brenner went further, predicting the shortest 12-round fight in history. He wasn’t far off.

Trainer Gil Clancy wanted Quarry to box, but Quarry abandoned that idea almost immediately. Instead of giving Shavers room to unleash his power, he attacked him.

Quarry drove Shavers toward the ropes and unloaded lefts and rights to the head. Shavers managed to move away, but Quarry followed him across the ring and dropped him with a left-right combination.

Shavers got back up, only to find Quarry waiting for him. Quarry poured on punches as Shavers struggled to defend himself. His eyes looked unfocused, and he was taking clean shots without answering effectively. Referee Arthur Mercante had seen enough and stopped the fight at 2:21 of the opening round. There would be no need for judges Jack Gordon and Bill Recht.

The result was stunning because Quarry had beaten the knockout artist by fighting him at his own game. George Foreman, Joe Frazier, and Muhammad Ali were among the prominent names at ringside. Foreman reportedly expressed surprise that Quarry had chosen to trade with Shavers and came away impressed by his aggression.

Ali and Frazier had another reason to be at the Garden. Their January 28, 1974 rematch was already set for the same arena and was promoted during the Quarry-Shavers telecast. Frazier discussed getting his weight down and preparing for Ali before the main event, while viewers were urged to buy tickets for their second fight.

Their rematch also strengthened Quarry’s position in the heavyweight picture. With Ali and Frazier committed to fighting each other, the broadcast team noted that neither man would likely be available for Foreman until around June. Quarry’s destruction of Shavers suddenly made him an obvious candidate to challenge the champion before then.

Quarry paid a physical price despite the short night. He injured his left wrist after landing a hook high on Shavers’ head, with reports raising concern over a possible fracture.

Shavers later admitted that the first heavy blows had left him unable to recover. He regretted rising so quickly after the knockdown, believing that taking more of the count might have given him enough time to survive the remaining seconds of the round.

Nearly 15,000 spectators had come expecting to see what happened when Shavers’ frightening power collided with Quarry’s durability and experience. They barely had time to settle into their seats.

The official attendance was 14,962, producing a gate of $201,564. Quarry was guaranteed $40,000 against 30 percent of the gate, while Shavers received $30,000 against 27½ percent.

The victory strengthened Quarry’s position near the top of a stacked division ruled by Foreman, but the championship opportunity never followed. Quarry instead met Frazier again the following year and was stopped in five rounds.

Shavers rebuilt his career and eventually challenged both Ali and Larry Holmes for the heavyweight championship.

Neither man’s later career changed what happened that December night. Shavers arrived with the reputation as a devastating slugger, but Quarry never gave him enough time to use it.

For 141 seconds, Quarry simply beat him to the punch.

Ghana News.title: Obuasi court remands 2 teachers over alleged attack on SHS headmaster
Ghana News.content:
The Obuasi Circuit Court has remanded two teachers of Obuasi Senior High Technical School into police custody for one week over allegations that they incited students to attack the school’s headmaster.

Kwasi Brefo, 41, and Joseph Appiah Arthur, 34, appeared before the court for the first time on Tuesday, August 11, 2026.

They have been charged with two counts of abetment under the Criminal and Other Offences Act, 1960.

The court has ordered the two teachers to reappear on August 17, 2026.

The prosecution told the court that the suspects aided and abetted students to cause unlawful damage to property belonging to the school.

They are also accused of instigating students to attack the headmaster, Abdulai Zakaria, on August 4.

Obuasi District Commander, Superintendent Mahama Iddrisu, had earlier told JoyNews that the two suspects were among three teachers arrested following a complaint from the headmaster.

Meanwhile, police are awaiting an autopsy and DNA examination on a male foetus exhumed from a location close to one of the school’s dormitories.

Superintendent Iddrisu said the foetus, which was discovered on August 5, is being kept at the morgue of the Obuasi Government Hospital.

The headmaster, Abdulai Iddrisu, who sustained machete injuries during the incident, has since been discharged from the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital.

Ghana News.title: Mason jailed eight years for robbing pharmacist
Ghana News.content:
The Kwadaso Circuit Court in the Ashanti Region has sentenced a 35-year-old mason to eight years’ imprisonment for robbing a pharmacist at Denchemuoso, near Kwadaso.

Michael Okyere, the convict, pleaded not guilty to the charge but was convicted after a full trial presided over by Jephthar Appau.

Police Chief Inspector David Opoku Kwabi, presenting the facts to the court, said the complainant, Ms Salomey Ametefe Enyonam, was an attendant at Kingsley Nsiah Chemist at Atwima Techiman, while the convict loitered around Denchemuoso.

He said on January 22, 2025, at about 0900 hours, the complainant reported for duty and about 15 minutes later, Okyere entered the shop and requested to see the doctor in charge.

According to the prosecution, the complainant asked him to wait while she called the doctor.

However, Okyere became aggressive, pushed her against a refrigerator in the office, forcibly took her iPhone 11 mobile phone valued at GH¢4,500.00 and fled.

The prosecution said the complainant raised an alarm, prompting some youths in the area to pursue and arrest the convict before handing him over to the Denchemuoso Police.

In his caution statement, Okyere admitted the offence and pleaded for leniency.

Following investigations, he was charged and arraigned before the court, which found him guilty after a full trial and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment.

Ghana News.title: Big Push probe: Presidential staffer challenges Fourth Estate’s report on Valerie Sawyerr committee
Ghana News.content:
Gilbert Attipoe is a presidential advisor at the Jubilee House

Presidential staffer Gilbert Atippoe has challenged the accuracy of a report by The Fourth Estate on the Presidential Committee’s investigation into sole-sourced contracts under the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme.

In March 2026, The Fourth Estate revealed how the Ministry of Roads and Highways had allegedly become a factory for sole-sourcing under the government’s Big Push initiative; it also published how contracts had been awarded to companies with questionable capacity and experience.

In a social media post on Tuesday, August 11, following the government's investigation into the allegations, Mr Atippoe says official records from state regulatory institutions contradict key claims contained in The Fourth Estate’s publication.

He argued that this raises questions about the basis on which the media organisation reached its conclusions.

In a detailed response, he defended the 72-page report produced by the committee chaired by Dr Valerie Sawyerr, insisting that its findings were based on statutory records and documentary evidence.

He rejected suggestions that the committee either deliberately published inaccurate information or was misled during its investigations.

Company registration

One of the issues Mr Atippoe raised concerns the registration history of Growth 82 Ventures.

According to him, records from the Office of the Registrar of Companies show that the company was incorporated on August 18, 2020, under registration number BN680822020.

He said the record contradicts any assertion that the company’s existence did not correspond with the timeline presented in the committee’s report.

“The official certificates from the Office of the Registrar of Companies confirm that Growth 82 Ventures was registered as far back as August 18, 2020,” Mr Atippoe said.

He further pointed to records from the Ministry of Roads and Highways concerning Growth 82 Global Ltd.

Mr Atippoe said the company holds an A1, B1 financial classification, which he described as the top-tier classification required for major infrastructure works.

He argued that this demonstrates that the company had the requisite statutory capacity to undertake major projects.

SSNIT records cited

The presidential staffer also disputed claims concerning the workforce capacity of contractors referenced in the committee’s report.

He cited SSNIT records relating to Build Managers Ltd and Sanam Ghana Ltd, saying the companies had active employee rolls of 20 and 26 workers respectively.

According to him, both companies also held valid SSNIT Clearance Certificates and had met their statutory obligations under the National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766).

Mr Atippoe said the records undermine concerns about whether the companies had the workforce capacity reflected in the committee’s assessment.

“These verifiable facts show that the committee’s assessments of company capacity were accurate and thorough,” he said.

Demand for correction

Mr Atippoe has subsequently accused The Fourth Estate of failing to conduct adequate verification of regulatory records before publishing its report.

He said the publication had unfairly cast doubt on the professional integrity of Dr Valerie Sawyerr and other members of the Presidential Committee.

“Basic journalistic ethics and public accountability dictate that when a media organisation publishes inaccurate premises that damage public reputations, a prompt correction is required,” he said.

He is therefore calling on The Fourth Estate to retract what he described as a misleading publication and issue an unreserved public apology to Dr Sawyerr and the members of the committee.

Ghana News.title: Since Gold Coast, national security has never faced an open trial – Atta Akyea
Ghana News.content:
Samuel Atta Akyea, Chairman of the the Parliamentary Select Committee on Mines and Energy, and MP for Abuakwa South

Lawyer for former National Signals Bureau (NSB) Director-General Kwabena Adu-Boahen, Samuel Atta Akyea, says the trial involving his client presents an unprecedented challenge because national security matters have historically not been subjected to open court proceedings.

Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Mr Atta Akyea said the case requires his personal involvement because of the sensitive national security issues at stake.

“I mean to come to terms with a case that since Guggisberg time or the Gold Coast, a national security matter has never been a subject matter of an open trial, you think it’s a small case that we are doing,” he said.

He argued that the proceedings could set a significant precedent for how Ghana handles national security matters in the courts.

“Dangerous president that, because of one man, let’s cancel the whole of the submarine tactics of national security and put national security on trial,” he said.

Mr Atta Akyea maintained that the case is too significant for him to delegate entirely to a junior lawyer in his chamber.

“I don’t think a junior, I mean, will be able to face such an unprecedented case coming from the Attorney General, so I couldn’t cede space to a junior to go and do this job for my client. With all respect,” he said.

His comments came as he also criticised what he described as selective justice in the handling of cases before the courts.

He questioned why some cases were being prioritised while murder, manslaughter, rape and other criminal cases remained pending.

“I keep asking why this selective justice is the Chief Justice trying to force on us?” he asked.

“All the murder cases, all the man-slaughter cases, all the rape cases and other criminal cases, that have happened does not have consequence at all,” he said.

According to him, the decision to expedite particular cases should not undermine established court procedures and practices.

“I believe that I’ve come far. I’m not a little boy in the game for me to use one case to cancel the traditions, the practices, and the statutory provisions of Ghana,” he said.

He also questioned why judges who had already begun hearing some cases should be directed to continue with them, despite other demands on lawyers appearing before them.

“So part-heard cases should continue, and these are without the reference to the programs of the lawyers, whether the lawyers who go abroad to do some good medication, or the lawyers who go to the national bar conference, or the lawyers who travel whatever,” he said.

The lawyer said the courts should not apply different standards to cases simply because some have attracted greater public attention.

“So I keep asking this question: What selective justice is the chief justice trying to force on us?” he asked.

Ghana News.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
Ghana News.content:
Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country inthe Middle East to formally end capital punishment.

A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it.

The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure.

Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row.

Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced.

Hard labour is alreadywritten intoLebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity.

The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law.

"We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC.

As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon.

"We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said.

Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004.

Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security.

Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008.

Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East.

Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017.

In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed.

Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023.

Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent".

In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month.

Ghana News.title: The rise of AI in the classroom: Balancing technological innovation with critical thinking
Ghana News.content:
Artificial intelligence is set to revolutionize education. From personalized learning and instant grading to AI tutors and essay-writing algorithms, technology has the power to fundamentally change what students learn, how they learn, and who does the teaching.



The rise of AI in education brings great promise to the classroom, but also presents one very important question: How can we integrate technology into the classroom while still ensuring that students develop critical thinking skills?

The answer to this question is complicated. But it should start with recognizing the value of using AI as a tool.

AI's Role in the Classroom



AI can be valuable to students and teachers. It is able to offer unique opportunities to enhance learning that couldn't have been possible before and can help to facilitate many time-consuming classroom tasks.

For students, AI can act as a brainstorming partner, tutor, writer, or research assistant. When done right, AI can make it much easier for students to learn, practice, and apply knowledge.



As for teachers, AI can help plan lessons, create practice exercises, organize information, design differentiated activities, and provide feedback. This could allow teachers to spend much less time on day-to-day activities, and more time discussing, creating, and interacting with students in the classroom.

But with all the benefits that generative AI could bring comes an equal amount of responsibility.

The Downfall of Thinking Skills



The main issue with AI in the classroom is that the thinking skills required to truly use it effectively can be bypassed.



If a computer is able to write an essay faster and more effectively than a student ever could, why should a student bother with the time consuming process of learning how to write a good essay?

This can allow for an artificial divide between using an AI algorithm to help a student think versus using an algorithm to do the thinking, and the latter is much more common than the former.



Education has traditionally revolved around teaching students to think critically, interpret, analyze, and creatively apply concepts.

If technology does too much of the thinking and problem solving for students, they might get much better grades while learning much less than before. Not only that, but students will be less likely to question or think critically about information that came directly from a computer.



AI's role in education could undermine the value of thinking skills, especially if students are overly reliant on it.

Furthermore, students also need to understand that just because a computer says something is true, doesn't mean that it is.

Students will need to become much more critical of the information given to them by artificial intelligence, especially given that it may not always be accurate.

Critical thinking is more important than ever in an age of AI



When given the choice between trusting an AI-generated fact and thinking critically about a situation, there are numerous important questions students should be able to ask themselves:



Is the information given true?



What are the sources that back this information up?



Did I phrase my question correctly so that the AI was able to understand and respond correctly?

Could there be any sort of bias or assumptions being made here?



What other information could there be?



How can I verify this information for myself?



This sort of questioning can be incorporated into education in a number of different ways, including by asking students to analyze AI-generated work for mistakes or biases or compare it to real information.

Instead of completely ruling out AI from education, critical thinking can also be integrated into teaching by teaching students to question the information that AI does provide.



How can Teachers Measure Learning?



The advent of generative AI introduces another major issue in education: assessment.



If a student is able to use AI to generate an essay, a mathematical proof, or even a lab report, how can teachers ensure that students are truly learning and applying the information they are being taught?

While it could be argued that essay writing, mathematical proofs, and lab reports have always been difficult tasks, their widespread use in education has become a limiting factor in the way that students are expected to learn.

Education should evolve to meet the needs of the times it's in, and if certain tasks can be made much easier and more efficient by AI, then it's important to ask whether or not these tasks should really matter that much.



It's not that these tasks have no place in education - clearly they do.



But with the advent of AI, it's important that education diversifies its assessment methods to incorporate not just written or mathematical tasks, but also oral presentations, project-based learning, or even in-class practice and writing exercises.



Assessments should also reflect how students reach conclusions as much as what those conclusions are. If students are able to cite their sources or show their work, it can become much more clear whether or not a student actually understood the material. Likewise, certain assignments should specifically encourage students to think through their work or show their reasoning. This includes reflective journal entries, drafting work, or even in-class or project-based assessments.



The Value of Teachers



While AI is set to revolutionize education, it's unlikely to fully replace the role of teachers.

Teachers provide students with the context and encouragement that many students need to become successful learners.



Additionally, teachers can often detect when a student is struggling with concepts or falling behind, which is much more difficult for AI-assisted practice exercises.



Furthermore, teachers can also act as discussion facilitators, encouraging students to collaborate and think through topics together.



The role of a teacher is also going to be much more important when it comes to teaching critical thinking.

While it may be easy to generate a well-written response from AI, teachers should encourage student questioning by making them explain their reasoning or what they've learned about a certain topic.

They can also ask students to defend their arguments or prove concepts by relying on what they've learned. The teacher can encourage critical thinking from students by asking more Socratic questions: Why do you think this? What would convince you otherwise? Can you prove this concept? What information haven't we considered?



Finally, it should be remembered that schools also have a responsibility to educate students on AI itself. The ways that AI works - including its limitations - should be explained to students.



Students should be informed of ethical issues such as bias, privacy, misinformation, and intellectual property. Students also need to be educated about proper uses of AI. A teacher could use it to brainstorm ideas with. But a student shouldn't use it to write an essay for them on an assignment that they're supposed to do themselves. Policies need to be clearly communicated to students so that they can take advantage of AI's educational benefits while avoiding its pitfalls.



The Importance of Equality



It's also important to note that while AI can have many educational benefits, it's only as useful as the person using it.



Students with access to the most resources will always be in a better position to benefit from education than others.



Schools must be aware that the introduction of AI could widen the existing achievement gap if certain students are more able to use AI than others.



It's important to make sure that technology is treated fairly in the classroom and doesn't become the reason why some students learn much more than others. At the same time, schools should protect students from any misuse of their personal information.



The Balance Between Learning and Technology



The issue of the balance between learning and technology is a fine line to walk.

Many argue that technology itself isn't inherently bad, but should also never be used at the expense of human skills such as critical thinking and learning. But how can we do both in the classroom while maximizing the benefits of both?



The answer lies in recognizing the balance between the two.

There's certainly a place in education for utilizing the potential of technology and maximizing its usefulness. But no matter how much technology is involved in education, critical thinking will always be the most valuable skill to learn.



Students need to learn how to think through and understand topics, especially when the information provided could be unreliable. They need to learn how to question information, research, organize, plan, and apply concepts. AI can help with all of these, but at the end of the day it's only a tool.



A student who uses AI to generate ten brainstorming ideas but then analyzes those ideas to find the best ones for an essay or speech is learning critical thinking. A student who uses AI to generate a fully formed research paper and turns it in as their own original work isn't really learning anything at all.

AI is becoming an increasingly prominent force in education, and its impact on the classroom is only set to grow.



Its potential to personalize learning, assist teachers, and provide instant feedback and practice opportunities is undeniably valuable.



But technology should never come at the cost of critical thinking, creativity, and learning.

Education should always be about building minds, challenging students, and encouraging them to think for themselves.



If AI is being introduced into the classroom, it needs to be done in a responsible way that doesn't compromise those values. The classroom of the future shouldn't be a race between human minds and artificial intelligence, but rather a collaboration that encourages learning from both.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: In Gaza’s tents, widows face war’s harshest realities alone
World.content:
Widows in Gaza struggle alone under displacement, burdened by loss, insecurity, and daily battles for survival.

Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Under the scorching heat inside a displacement tent in northern Gaza, Mona al-Masri tries to plan for each day as it comes.

Mona is a widow, and the mother of four children, ranging in age from nine to two. Her husband, Mohammed, was killed in an Israeli strike in September 2024.

Between fabric walls that provide little protection, Mona carries the responsibilities of a family burdened by displacement brought on by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying loss of security.

Mona begins each morning trying to secure her family’s basic needs, searching for water, arranging food, and attempting to protect her children from a reality that no longer resembles the life they knew before the war began in 2023. She says that what hurts her most is not only the harshness of their living conditions, but also the feeling that she has been forced to confront every detail of daily life alone.

“There is no normal life inside the tent. Every day begins with the same questions: how will we secure our needs, and how will we get through another day surrounded by this exhaustion?” Mona says. “The war did not only take away our homes; it took away our sense of safety and stability and made even the simplest things require enormous effort.”

Rising numbers

Mona is one of thousands of women in the Gaza Strip who have found themselves facing new roles imposed by the war, taking care of their families by themselves.



According to data from the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, the total number of widows in the Gaza Strip has risen to more than 50,000. The figure includes 28,224 women who became widows as a result of the war, in addition to more than 22,500 widows who were already registered with the ministry before the war.

Aziza al-Kahlout, spokesperson for the Ministry of Social Development in Gaza, says the number is expected to rise further because not all widows have yet been registered.

“The war has left these women facing a difficult reality, including the responsibility of supporting their families without a provider, amid widespread destruction and the collapse of the basic conditions needed for a decent life,” al-Kahlout says.

“This requires effective programmes for economic empowerment, job creation and strengthening self-reliance to help lift them out of poverty and deprivation,” she says.

Al-Kahlout stresses that widows’ needs extend beyond financial assistance. They also require psychological and social support, healthcare, and legal assistance related to guardianship, custody, financial rights and inheritance.

“Protecting and empowering widows in the Gaza Strip has become a shared national and humanitarian responsibility that requires an urgent and sustainable response,” al-Kahlout says.

She explains that widows need regular financial assistance, emergency relief, psychosocial and healthcare services, legal support and educational opportunities, in addition to vocational training and support for small and family businesses.

Psychological support

The loss of a husband during the war has not only deprived thousands of women of their life partners, but has also been accompanied by displacement, the destruction of homes, and the loss of stability.

Aseel Abu Shaweesh, a psychologist, explains that losing a husband during war represents a traumatic experience with profound psychological and social impacts on widows and their children. She notes that many women who lost their husbands have found themselves facing new and increasing responsibilities while simultaneously dealing with their other troubles.

“A widow in Gaza faces the pain of losing her husband, the responsibility of supporting her family, and caring for her children in an environment filled with fear and instability,” Abu Shaweesh says.

She adds: “Many women are forced to hide their grief and emotional collapse so they can carry on in front of their children, while the accumulation of daily pressures and the lack of space to express their pain increase levels of anxiety and psychological exhaustion.”



Abu Shaweesh explains that children in families who have lost one parent are also deeply affected, especially when the loss of the father is accompanied by displacement and deteriorating living conditions.

“A child loses their father and their sense of safety and stability. They may show signs of constant fear, sleep disturbances, and behavioural changes as a result of the difficult experiences they have endured,” Abu Shaweesh says.

The psychologist emphasises that widows’ needs include financial assistance as well as psychological and social support services to help them adapt to the new roles imposed by the war.

“These women need continuous support that helps them regain a sense of safety and the ability to manage their lives and their families under these difficult circumstances,” she says.

World.title: Fishermen face deadly dangers as Yemen’s Red Sea becomes a warzone
World.content:
Many Yemeni fishermen have abandoned the trade, seeking safer livelihoods as Red Sea becomes too dangerous.

Al-Makha, Yemen – Mazhar works on a sea that has long been a front line in Yemen’s conflict.

The fisherman, based in the city of al-Makha (also known as Mocha) on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, has long struggled to make a living since war arrived in the region in 2015.

Fuel is expensive, and so is renting a boat. But Mazhar, who is in his 40s and has a family that solely relies on the income from his fishing, has a bigger problem: whenever he sets out for the sea, he might not return home.

“Recently, a fishing boat in al-Khawkhah was fired on, and we lost two colleagues,” Mazhar said. “No one knows why, and the authorities haven’t announced the cause of the incident.”

Venturing beyond the shoreline is a dangerous gamble since the sea turned into a battlefield – Mazhar knows fishermen who have gone missing without a trace. But when there’s no food left at home, he decides to risk it anyway.

Red Sea restrictions

Yemen’s Red Sea coast is one of the main hubs of the country’s fishing industry, which before the war was the country’s second-largest source of export earnings after oil.

The Red Sea fishing industry has been impacted since the early years of the war, with fish exports from the region falling by about 70 percent, according to a 2018 study.

The region is strategically important for other reasons, too. Yemen’s principal port of Hodeidah sits about 160 kilometres (100 miles) up the coast from al-Makha, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait lies at its southern entrance, controlling entry into one of the world’s most vital waterways. All of that means that the coastline has been heavily contested since the early days of the war.



Currently, the Houthi rebels control most of the territory from Yemen’s border with Saudi Arabia down to Hodeidah, with pro-government forces, largely the Guardians of the Republic force, operating south of the port city. The front line had been quiet in recent years, but recent Houthi attacks against pro-government forces across the country have also targeted al-Makha.

But it is events in the waters of the Red Sea that have drawn the most attention internationally. The Houthis began regularly striking shipping passing through the region after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, and have also recently attacked Saudi shipping. The attacks have prompted the United States, the United Kingdom, Israel and Saudi Arabia to strike Houthi targets in Yemen at various times, including on the Red Sea.

Mazhar explained that fishermen now face strict boundaries at sea that they cannot cross. That is not only the case in al-Makha, but also in neighbouring al-Khawkhah district and large parts of the entire Red Sea coast.

“We pay money to buy scrap barrels and car bodies to dump into the sea to form artificial reefs. However, with every escalation in the Red Sea, we are denied access to our reefs for military reasons and are forced to fish near the shore,” Mazhar said.

Threats

“I cannot name the party restricting us right now because I am a fisherman, and speaking out could put me at risk,” Mazhar said. “But both warring sides have prevented us from sailing at different times. We are the victims of every faction fighting in our area.”

Before 2018, local fishermen say that the National Resistance Force (which the Guardians of the Republic forces later emerged out of) prevented fishermen from venturing into deep waters and reaching their reefs. Although restrictions were later eased, the fishermen say that both the Houthis and pro-government forces have placed restrictions on sailing since 2023.

“In the end, it is the fishermen who suffer to provide for their families,” Mazhar said. “We have no hand in this war, yet we bear its worst consequences.”

He added that several of his fellow fishermen have been arrested after being accused of smuggling or aiding one faction against another – claims he says are completely unfounded.

Akram, who also works as a fisherman in al-Makha, describes another danger: sea mines.

“Last year, I left home alongside two of my neighbours, and a sea mine exploded under their boat near the shore in al-Khawkhah,” he recalled. “It’s a sea mine; how can we avoid it? I can say with certainty that the Red Sea is no longer safe, and we have to move elsewhere.”



“We are witnessing the worst days in the Red Sea,” Akram added. “To be a fisherman in the Red Sea, you must carry your shroud on your shoulders.”

Fouad Doubla, head of the Fishermen’s Association in al-Khawkhah, told Al Jazeera that more than 30,000 fishermen have been affected by the conditions on the Red Sea coast and are struggling to provide basic necessities for their families, as fishing is their sole source of income.

Doubla noted that 113 fishermen have gone missing in the Red Sea since 2023, with their families receiving no information about their whereabouts. He added that the presence of sea mines is a direct consequence of the war that continuously threatens fishermen’s lives.

“Sea mines have killed 264 fishermen and maimed 215 others, forcing many to stop fishing and look for alternative work,” Doubla said, adding fishermen had also been detained by pirates in the Red Sea.

Alternative choices

Doubla explained that the difficulties and dangers encountered by fishermen have many looking for a different way to make money.

“When fishermen realised they could no longer sail safely and that their families lacked food, they were left with no choice but to either risk their lives at sea or find another job – and many chose the latter to stay safe,” Doubla said.

For Akram, that means relocating to Aden, where he believes fishing on Yemen’s southern coastline will be safer.

“Nothing is worth risking our lives for. The families of those who were lost are now struggling just to find enough food. I encourage my colleagues to join me and move to a safe area.”

Ismail, a 48-year-old who comes from a long line of fishermen, decided to leave the profession behind entirely last year, selling the gear he had collected over 20 years and using the proceeds to buy a minibus instead.

“Danger surrounds fishermen from every direction, and we never know when we will meet our fate at sea,” Ismail told Al Jazeera while holding the steering wheel of his minibus. “I don’t think any wise man would continue fishing amid such danger.”

Ismail’s wife supported his decision to quit fishing and sold some of her jewellery to help him start his new business, relieved to end the constant anxiety she and their five children felt whenever he went out to sea.

“Sometimes we stayed at sea for four days, which was completely normal under regular circumstances,” Ismail said. “But nowadays, it isn’t safe. When I stayed out for more than a day, my family would panic, and I think they had every right to be worried.”

Today, Ismail earns a modest income driving his minibus, but he is content knowing he is safe and able to share every meal with his family without constant fear.

Mazhar, who continues to fish close to their shore, believes those who transitioned to new jobs have made the right choice.

“I’ve thought more than once about leaving this dangerous profession, but I have no alternative,” he said. “As soon as I find one, I won’t hesitate for a second.”
