Azerbaijan officially declared neutrality, repeatedly stressed its support for Iran’s sovereignty and said its territory was not being used against third countries. However, several international media outlets, including CNN, reported that Israeli special forces and intelligence structures were allegedly deployed on Azerbaijani territory during the war. Baku called these claims “completely unfounded”.

Several think tanks, including the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), described Azerbaijan’s position as a “carefully maintained balance between its officially declared neutrality and practical rapprochement”. Turkey’s decision not to take part in the war and its advice to Baku to maintain a cautious position also influenced this approach.

This dynamic takes on additional significance in the context of the Mecca agreement. The agreement’s principle that “an attack on one is an attack on all”, along with Saudi Arabia’s response to Iranian strikes during the war, shows how collective defence commitments can operate during periods of real tension. Azerbaijan’s deep strategic partnership with Israel, its allied relations with Turkey and Pakistan, and its expanding ties with Saudi Arabia have led some experts to believe that this rapprochement could increase Baku’s interest in formats similar to the Mecca agreement.

For Azerbaijan, therefore, the main question is not so much whether to join the agreement, but how to benefit from closer ties among its existing partners – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Israel – without taking on formal commitments. This is precisely the flexibility that its multi-vector policy provides.

Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

World.title: Number of Iranian companies in Georgia up 510% since 2012 – EPRC
World.content:
Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

According to data from the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the number of Iranian companies in Georgia has increased by around 510% since 2012, exceeding 12,800 by 2025–26.

EPRC says the figures are based on data from Geostat and the National Bank of Georgia. The organisation also notes that despite the sharp rise in the number of companies, foreign direct investment from Iran into Georgia has remained relatively low in recent years.

“Between 2013 and 2024, Iranian investment totalled $41 million. Although this is more than in the previous period, the amount per company remains quite small,” EPRC said.

According to the organisation, net foreign direct investment from Iran stood at -$0.65 million in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2025 put the figure at around $0.4 million.

EPRC estimates that Iran’s share of total foreign direct investment in Georgia remains small, according to official statistics.

The centre says Iranian companies registered in Georgia are mainly involved in small-scale trade, real estate transactions, services, construction, logistics and re-export.

“Most of this activity involves small and medium-sized businesses and is less connected to large-scale manufacturing, industrial or technology projects,” EPRC said.

The organisation notes that the activities of these companies have not led to significant job creation. It also says that dozens of companies are often registered at the same address.

According to EPRC, tourism has seen the most notable growth in economic activity linked to Iran. Between 2022 and 2024, tourism revenues from Iran rose from $91.1 million to $151.1 million, an increase of 65%. However, tourism revenues fell by 17.8% in 2025.

Why the number of Iranian companies is growing much faster than investment

The centre believes that the rapid increase in the number of companies, alongside relatively low levels of investment and official financial flows, raises questions about the true scale of their activities.

“Why is the number of Iranian companies growing much faster than investment and official financial inflows overall?” EPRC asks.

The organisation says that, given that a significant part of Iran’s financial sector operates under international sanctions, economic transactions may be taking place through alternative and potentially less transparent financial channels.

EPRC notes that if some economic activity takes place outside the traditional banking system or with limited transparency, this makes it harder for the state to effectively monitor financial flows. It also increases the risks of sanctions evasion and money laundering.

The centre also points to international practice, where such models are sometimes associated with nominal or so-called “paper” companies. These companies are officially registered, but their actual economic activity may be very limited.

According to EPRC, such companies are sometimes used for re-export operations, intermediary financial transactions, or to circumvent sanctions and regulatory requirements in different countries.

“When the number of companies grows rapidly but this is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in investment, production, exports or employment, questions arise about the real economic significance of their activities,” the organisation said.

EPRC also points to the visa-free regime between Georgia and the EU, saying that this could make the country more attractive to Iranian citizens and businesses.

According to the centre, the US sanctions imposed on Shelbit, a cryptocurrency company registered in Georgia and owned by an Iranian citizen, highlight the range of possible ways to circumvent sanctions.

EPRC believes that, in light of this case and the sharp increase in the number of companies opened in Georgia by Iranian citizens, the current figures should be viewed with additional risks in mind.

Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi’s new zoo ready to welcome visitors – video
World.content:
The new Tbilisi Zoo will open to visitors in August 2026. Construction began after the 2015 floods, and the zoo is opening in stages. Although work is still under way, visitors will soon be able to explore the new site.

One of Tbilisi Zoo’s best-known residents, Shani the lion cub, has already moved to the new zoo.

___________________________________________

___________________________________________

As David Taktakishvili, deputy director of Tbilisi Zoo, explains, the new zoo covers a large area, and the site is being developed in stages. Some animals have already been moved, but construction of the enclosures is still under way. Construction and infrastructure work will therefore continue after the zoo opens.

The zoo administration believes the public should already have the opportunity to see for themselves how a new-generation zoo is taking shape and how much better the animals will live in their new environment.

When the new zoo opens to visitors, the Caucasus biogeographical zone will be accessible to the public. In the future, the zoo will bring together spaces representing different regions of the world. At the first stage, however, the focus will be on the local flora and fauna of the Caucasus. Visitors will see red deer, bison, bears, wolves and other local species in this zone.

Construction of the African zone is currently under way. The new zoo will gradually add other biogeographical zones in the future.

In recent years, the role of zoos has also changed significantly. Today, one of their main functions is nature conservation, including protecting, breeding and caring for endangered species. The new, modern facility will serve this purpose and, in the future, will become not only a place for visitors but also an important wildlife conservation centre.

Admission prices will remain unchanged: free for children under three, 2 lari ($0.76) for children aged three to 12, and 4 lari ($1.53) for visitors aged 12 and over.

Some animals will remain at the old zoo, which will continue to operate as usual.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

New Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgian opposition figure investigated for ‘treason’ over comments on Abkhazia war
World.content:
Giorgi Baramidze case

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into comments by Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, about the war in Abkhazia. The case concerns charges of treason and actions that threaten state interests. The investigation focuses on his account of how prisoners of war were treated during the early stages of the conflict. Baramidze made the comments on a podcast, triggering a political backlash. The de facto authorities in Abkhazia have also reacted to his remarks.

What did Baramidze say?

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, discussed the war in Abkhazia on Yago Khvichia’s “Birth of Georgia” programme.

Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, he said:

“We did not take prisoners, we had no prisoners, we executed them.”

The remark prompted a strong reaction from government officials. Baramidze later clarified several times what he meant.

He said he was referring to the early stages of the war, when the Georgian side did not yet have a regular and organised army. Baramidze later explained that people enraged by the deaths of their relatives in the fighting did not take enemy fighters prisoner.

“At first, the situation was as follows: people who were enraged after their mothers, fathers and relatives had been killed did not take prisoners during the fighting but killed them instead. That is the bitter truth about the early stages of the war. I know this because I personally took part in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze said.

According to him, the situation later changed. The Georgian side began taking prisoners, which made exchanges possible. Baramidze said that around 200 Georgian prisoners were eventually brought home as a result.

“My deputy and I could not have exchanged 200 Georgian prisoners if our side had not taken any prisoners at all,” he added.

Baramidze also denies that his comments were directed against the Georgian army or the state as a whole. He insists that he was referring specifically to the situation during the early stages of the war.

At the same time, he stressed Russia’s responsibility, saying that the Russian Federation acted as an aggressor and occupier in the wars of 1992–93 and 2008.

Why has the prosecutor’s office opened an investigation?

Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office opened the investigation at the request of the State Service of Veterans Affairs.

According to the agency, prosecutors are investigating the case under Articles 307¹ and 318 of the Criminal Code. The first concerns treason, while the second covers actions that threaten Georgia’s state interests.

The prosecutor’s office said:

“The investigation began following an appeal from the State Service of Veterans Affairs concerning comments made by Giorgi Baramidze, a member of the United National Movement. The case concerns his remarks about the war in Abkhazia and the prisoner exchange process, which he made on Yago Khvichia’s programme ‘Birth of Georgia’.”

As part of the investigation, prosecutors also summoned Koba Kobaladze, head of the State Service of Veterans Affairs, for questioning.

Baramidze sees the investigation as political persecution.

“The prosecutor’s office has opened a case against me for ‘betraying Georgia’! I am not afraid of your persecution, let alone your dirty propaganda!” he wrote on social media.

What does the government say?

Members of the Georgian Dream party do not consider Baramidze’s remarks simply an unfortunate choice of words. They argue that such statements could harm Georgia’s national interests and international standing.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described Baramidze’s comments as morally unacceptable. As for the legal assessment, he said the relevant authorities should make that decision.

“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: Solicitor accused of manufacturing illegal 3D-printed firearms
World.content:
A solicitor from Moree, in north-west NSW, has been charged with 16 offences including manufacturing prohibited firearms.

The 32-year-old man was arrested yesterday during a police firearm prohibition order compliance check at a Sunnyside Road home.

The 32-year-old solicitor was charged with 16 offences. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The State Crime Command's Drug and Firearm squad established Strike Force Temarang to investigate the importation and manufacture of 3D-printed and prohibited firearms.

Police allegedly seized a bolt-action rifle, two pistols, a semi-automatic privately manufactured firearm, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and ammunition manufacturing equipment during the search.

Police will also allege hundreds of rounds of ammunition were seized. (Supplied: NSW Police )

Following the man's arrest, police searched a second property at Frome Street, allegedly seizing a 3D printer, blueprints to create firearms and electronic devices.

Inquiries into the manufacture of 3D printed firearms commenced in Moree in April this year. (Supplied: NSW Police )

The man will face court today.

World.title: CIT CEO Margot McNeill awarded about $445,000 upon resignation
World.content:
The board chair of the Canberra Institute of Technology Tom Rogers says Margot McNeill received about $445,000 upon her resignation yesterday after months of controversy.

Her appointment as chief executive in June 2025 was questioned earlier this year after revelations she had failed to disclose an investigation into misconduct in her previous role at TAFE NSW.

In May, Dr McNeill came under further pressure to resign after an ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry found she "should have disclosed the information about the misconduct investigation or findings to the CIT board in a timely manner and that she did not".

Today, Mr Rogers said Dr McNeill had been awarded the settlement but would not be drawn on whether the board had asked her to step down.

"She's left, she's resigned, we've accepted the resignation and that's the main thing," he said.

"And now we need to make sure that we are moving on and providing the sort of quality education which we are doing to students."

Canberra Institute of Technology board chair Tom Rogers says they are focusing on providing quality education as they move forward. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

In a statement about her resignation, Dr McNeill said it had been a difficult decision to resign from the "much-loved Canberra institution".

"It has become clear that this decision is in the best interest of the CIT community, especially students and staff, about whom I care deeply. Equally, it is in my best interest, including that of my family."

Throughout the saga, Dr McNeill has repeatedly said she was under strict obligation not to share the existence of the investigation with her previous employer, but TAFE NSW has publicly refuted that.

Her evidence before the initial committee triggered another assembly probe exploring whether Dr McNeill had misled the assembly.

Released last week, its findings criticised her as having been "deliberately obstructive" and "combative".

Dr McNeill's legal case against TAFE NSW is ongoing in the NSW Supreme Court and she has been on extended leave throughout the controversy.

On Friday last week, Mitch Pirie was appointed acting chief executive of CIT.

CIT to focus on 'quality education': board chair

Mr Rogers told ABC Radio Canberra this morning that Dr McNeill's resignation was a "good outcome".

"It does draw a line on a lot of speculation over the last few months," he said.

He said they were looking to move forward and "rebuild the CIT's reputation".

Asked if Dr McNeill was asked by the board to step down, Mr Rogers said there had been a "process".

"There was a process and she announced her resignation and we've accepted her resignation," he said.

"That matter is now dealt with and we're able to draw a line on that and move forward."

Margot McNeill resigned on Tuesday, saying it was in the best interests of staff, students and her family. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Rogers said the approximately $445,000 payout was the "figure that was agreed on after looking at a whole range of factors".

"I think the exact figure is $445,000 or something like that," he said.

He also spoke about how the board had handled Dr McNeill's recruitment prior to his appointment.

Without saying he would criticise or defend the board's approach to Dr McNeill's hiring, he said a report had found they had "gone above and beyond" during that process.

"I came in ... at the end of March, I've been dealing with a complex issue," he said.

"This is not a one-off, this is a long period of some disruption at CIT.

"What I want to try now is to steady that ship and to move it forward."

The Canberra Institute of Technology gained an acting chief executive amid investigations into the hiring of Margot McNeill. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Resignation a 'relief': Emerson

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said Ms McNeill's resignation had come as a "relief".

"I think this is an outcome that's going to be welcomed by many staff at CIT and by the broader community here in the ACT that deserves assurances our taxpayer funds are being used appropriately," he said on ABC Radio Canberra this morning."

Mr Emerson used parliamentary privilege to make claims of professional misconduct against the Electric Vehicle TAFE Centre of Excellence in May, disclosed to him by a whistleblower.

He was also Pressure increases on CIT CEO to stand down after it was revealed she was being investigated over allegations of "serious misconduct" at the time of her CIT hiring.

"This is something I've been calling for the last four months since it became clear that she had failed to disclose misconduct findings made against her by her former employer on a fit and proper persons declaration to the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator ASQA," he said.

"And since then we've had an Assembly committee find that she actively misled her board.

"Another Assembly committee raised serious concerns about her conduct and recommend they be investigated by the Public Sector Standards Commissioner."

The Public Sector Standards Commissioner yesterday confirmed they had "received a referral of disclosable conduct investigation" on July 30 relating to CIT's use of rental electric vehicles in the training of student mechanics.

"The matter relates to the Canberra Institute of Technology Electric Vehicle TAFE Centre of Excellence training program, and an investigation has commenced in accordance with the requirements of the PID Act," they said in a statement.

CIT chief executive Margot McNeill had previously described the allegations as "factually incorrect" and "offensive".

Mr Emerson said that, as a public institution, CIT now needed to consider real governance reform.

"I think we need to not just tinker around the edges when it comes to governance reform, but look at a real overhaul of how things are run because current arrangements have clearly demonstrated over the last decade not to be working," he said.

World.title: Everything you need to know as Australia hosts Bangladesh in the Top End
World.content:
Australia is hosting Bangladesh in a rare Test series this August, as winter cricket hits the Top End.

The two teams will play two Tests, the first of which gets underway in Darwin on August 13 at Marrara Stadium.

The second starts on August 22 in Mackay, where Harrup Park will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia.

You can listen to live coverage of both Tests on the ABC Listen App, or follow the ABC Sport live blog.

'Nowhere to hide' or free swing?: ABC Cricket Podcast

It is the first time in 23 years that Bangladesh will tour Australia for a Test series.

Here's everything you need to know.

When does Australia play Bangladesh?

The first Test gets underway on Thursday, August 13, with the first session starting at 10am ACST in Darwin, NT.

That means the start time is 10:30am AEST (Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania), 10:00am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8:30am in Western Australia.

The second Test starts on Saturday, August 22, with the first ball again set to be bowled 10:00am AEST in Mackay, Queensland.

That is 10am in Queensland, New South Wales, ACT, Victoria and Tasmania, 10:30am in South Australia and the Northern Territory, and 8am in Western Australia.

Each Test is scheduled for five days.

Where are the Tests being played?

Australia played South Africa at Marrara Stadium last year in a T20 international. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

August is not normally cricket season in Australia, but officials are taking advantage of the dry season in the north to take these matches to the tropics, with Darwin and Mackay hosting the Test matches.

Darwin's Marrara Oval will host just its third ever men's Test match and first since Sri Lanka visited in July 2004.

Australia have a 100 per cent winning record in Tests in Darwin, winning by an innings and 132 runs against Bangladesh in 2003, following that up with a 149-run victory against Sri Lanka the year after.

Australia has also played four ODIs in Darwin, all against Bangladesh and all resulting in emphatic victories.

In T20Is it's a slightly different story though, with South Africa sharing the spoils across two matches at the venue last year.

Mackay's Harrup Park has never hosted a men's Test match before and will become the 12th venue in Australia to do so.

Harrup Park in Mackay will become the 12th ground to host a men's Test match in Australia. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The ground did host a youth Test match last year between Australia and India's under 19 sides, a low-scoring match won by India by seven wickets.

There have been three ODIs at the ground, two of them involving Australia. Again, South Africa were the opponents in 2025 and, again, the spoils were shared.

The only other ODI took place during the 1992 Cricket World Cup between India and Sri Lanka.

Given that Mackay averages 313.2 millimetres of rain in February — the wettest month on average across the year for the city — it's perhaps not a surprise that rain meant that the match was abandoned after just two balls were bowled.

That was even after a helicopter hovered above the pitch in an attempt to dry it out.

Australia's women have played three ODIs (in 2021) and two T20Is (in 2024) at the ground, winning all but one game.

Who is playing?

Pat Cummins returns for Australia's first Test of the season. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Australia has named a strong squad, with front-line bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all returning following their injury lay offs.

Such impressive bowling depth has seen Michael Neser miss out, the luckless Queenslander then suffering a hamstring injury in any case that will keep him out of contention.

It is, essentially, a full strength team, something Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto, is pretty impressed about.

"I personally liked the fact that they have chosen their full-strength team," he said earlier this month in an interview with ESPN Cricinfo.

"They are not taking us lightly. I think our team has earned this respect."

Najmul Hossain Shanto will lead Bangladesh in Australia. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Disappointingly for Bangladesh, they come into the series missing two key weapons in lightning-fast seamer Nahid Rana, who has been ruled out due to a left-side strain, and Shoriful Islam, who has a hurt hamstring.

Then, key spin bowler Taijul Islam suffered a blow to the hand in the warm up game and did not bowl at all in the second innings.

The 23-year-old Rana is one of the form bowlers in world cricket, capable of delivering the ball at speeds in excess of 150km/h. He has already taken 44 wickets in international cricket this year — the most by any bowler — at an average of 18.31.

On a positive note, Litton Das recovered from a calf injury he picked up during the home ODI series against Australia in June.

Batting is a problem for the tourists though — chief selector Habibul Bashar said the selection of 33-year-old lefty Soumya Sarkar was as a result of "a bit of desperation". Hardly a ringing endorsement for a man who has not played Test cricket since 2021.

Australia Squad Bangladesh Squad Pat Cummins (c) Najmul Hossain Shanto (c) Scott Boland Amite Hasan (wk) Alex Carey (wk) Ebadot Hossain Cameron Green Hasan Mahmud Josh Hazlewood Jaker Ali (wk) Travis Head Khaled Ahmed Josh Inglis (wk) Litton Das (wk) Marnus Labuschagne Mehidy Hasan Miraz Nathan Lyon Mominul Haque Steven Smith Musfik Hasan Mitchell Starc Mushfiqur Rahim (wk) Jake Weatherald Shadman Islam Beau Webster Soumya Sarkar Taijul Islam Tanzid Hasan Taskin Ahmed

Jake Weatherald, the first Northern Territorian to play a Test for Australia, was watching on in the crowd the last time the Australians played in Darwin.

He is a great chance to start on his home ground after a solid spell in the County Championship with Leicestershire, where he scored 483 runs at an average of 60.37, including scoring an unbeaten 104 against Glamorgan in Cardiff.

What form are Bangladesh in?

Bangladesh have only lost one of their last five Test matches. (Getty Images: Sameera Peiris)

Bangladesh come into this Test series off the back of a pretty decent run, having lost just one of their last five matches in the format.

Two thumping victories at home against Ireland in November 2025 were backed up by a hugely impressive 2-0 series victory against Pakistan in May this year.

That wasn't bad.

Now for the things that have been pretty poor.

A one off Test against Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club resulted in a calamitous defeat by an innings and 85 runs.

If that was bad, then the absolute thrashing the Cricket Australia XI delivered last week was even worse, the tourists bowled out for just 54 in their second dig as the CA XI won by an innings and 38 runs.

If it wasn't for Mehidy Hasan Miraz's unbeaten century in the first innings, rescuing his side from 6-110, who knows how bad the score would have looked as Corey Rocchiccioli took 6-83 in that first innings and Campbell Thompson took 8-25 in the second.

What is Bangladesh's record against Australia?

Jason Gillespie's stunning double century will go down in the annals as one of the best ever night watchman displays. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Bangladesh have only ever played against Australia six times in their Test history — they've only played fewer Tests against Ireland (3) and Afghanistan (2) which, given Bangladesh have been a Test-playing nation since 2000, is a damning inditement on Australia's commitment to playing the minnows.

Somewhat surprisingly then, Bangladesh does have a Test victory against Australia to their name and, it was their most recent series in 2017.

Bangladesh claimed a stunning 20-run victory in Mirpur, with Shakib Al Hasan claiming player of the match honours after scoring a 133-ball 84 in the first innings and taking 5-85 with the ball in the final innings.

Australia got revenge in Chattogram, winning by seven wickets as Nathan Lyon took 7-94 and 6-60, while David Warner scored a brilliant, six-hour, 234-ball 123 in the first innings.

Australia's best ever batting performance in Chattogram though came 11 years before that, when night watchman Jason Gillespie scored a stunning unbeaten 201 to help Australia claim victory by an innings and 80 runs.

The first Test of that series in Fatullah had been won by the far more tense margin of three wickets, with Ricky Ponting's grinding 118 not out helping the Aussies over the line.

Bangladesh have never beaten Australia in Australia though, losing both their 2003 Tests by over an innings, in matches that took place in Darwin and Cairns.

World.title: What happens if you forgot to do the census last night?
World.content:
Have you completed the census yet?

Technically, census night was last night, but that doesn't mean you've missed the boat.

What happens if you don't do the census?

Don't worry, you can still complete the census.

"There is still time to complete your form after census night," an Australian Bureau of Statistics spokesperson said.

Get to it as soon as you can and you shouldn't have a problem.

When is the census due?

As soon as possible.

Census night was on August 11, but this doesn't mean people had to complete the census on that exact date.

It just means you have to answer questions about where you were on the night of August 11.

More than five million Australian households completed their forms early this year and the ABS expects quite a few households to submit their forms after census night.

A report about the 2021 census said the online census form was open for about 10 weeks.

And paper forms were accepted "for as long as practicable", with the last paper form included in the census received in December 2021.

That was months after the 2021 census night in early August.

Census night was on August 11, but you're able to complete your form after that date. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

Do I have to do the census?

Yes, participating in the census is compulsory under the Census and Statistics Act 1905.

But you may not have to fill out a form yourself if someone in your household includes you and your information on the household form.

Almost everyone who is in Australia on census night must be included on a census form, including international students, visitors, visa holders and babies.

However, foreign diplomats and their families living in Australia are not included.

Is there a fine for not doing the census?

Yes, but that doesn't mean you'll be fined for being a few days late.

The ABS will contact you to encourage you to complete and submit your form first.

"We aim to get everyone to participate in the census voluntarily," an ABS spokesperson said.

If you don't respond to this gentle nudge, the ABS may serve you with a written direction to complete the census.

This is a formal legal instruction and if you fail to comply, you could be prosecuted and fined.

What is the fine for not doing the census?

If you're prosecuted for failing to comply with the legal instruction to complete the census, you could be fined up to $364 a day.

But remember, it doesn't have to come to that.

While we're on the topic of fines, it's also an offence to knowingly provide false or misleading statements or information in the census.

If you're prosecuted for this, you could face a fine of up to $3,640.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics aims to have people complete the census voluntarily. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

What is the point of the census?

The data gathered from the census is really important.

It helps the government plan for the future.

Information collected via the census helps the government make decisions about things like health care, transport, schools and infrastructure.

How often is the census?

Every five years.

The last one was in 2021.

Worried about what happens to your answers?

The personal information you give on your census form is confidential and protected by law.

It is not shared with anyone else outside the ABS.

This means government agencies like the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and Centrelink cannot see what you have written on your census form.

The data is handled by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which is an independent statutory authority and an official organisation trusted by 90 per cent of the general community, according to an ABS survey last year.

"We have a range of processes and protections that make sure information on census forms stays confidential," an ABS spokesperson said.

"For example, we use the strongest encryption technology available to make sure information from the online census form is secure.

"People should be reassured that organisations [other government departments and marketing companies] can't access any personal information you include on your census form."

The legislation around the census also imposes strict secrecy obligations on all ABS employees.

What if I don't want my household to see my answers?

You are allowed to fill out your own form, separate to your household.

All you need to do is call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 and someone will either provide you with a census number to complete your Census online or send you your own paper form.

The ABS keeps the form with the most complete information about the person, so answer as many questions as you can in your separate form.

"To ensure your separate form is counted, we ask that you use the same name, date of birth and sex recorded at birth details as those recorded on the household form where possible," an ABS spokesperson said.

"You can then respond to other questions on the census form in the way that best reflects you."

Can I do the census online?

Yes.

You can either fill out a paper form or complete it on the ABS Census website.

The website should look like this:

The online census portal is available on the Australian Bureau of Statistics website. (Australian Bureau of Statistics)

You will need your census number to complete the form online.

Where do I find my census number?

Your home should have received an envelope from the ABS that looks like this:

Look for the Australian Bureau of Statistics logo and orange text. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

Inside, there should be a letter containing a census number and a temporary password.

But if you don't have a census number, you can go to this website, where you'll be prompted to enter your mobile phone number so the ABS can text you a one-time PIN and your census number.

For help over the phone, you can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

World.title: 'Rude to say no': All Blacks icon performs solo haka against current team
World.content:
South African rugby teams love facing the haka. None have ever replied to New Zealand's traditional pre-match challenge with another haka until today.

Ma'a Nonu stepped in front of his new Sharks teammates and performed a solo haka in what will probably be the lasting memory of a tour match the New Zealanders won 54-0 at soggy Kings Park.

Nonu played 103 matches for New Zealand from 2003-15 and has continued playing around the world at age 44. The Sharks signed him a week ago to help develop their young players. Then as their injury list lengthened they drafted him onto the bench to face the All Blacks.

He was reluctant at first. He didn't want to detract from the Sharks' first match against the All Blacks in 30 years. He relented to help make up the numbers.

"I thought it would be rude to say no," Nonu told broadcaster SuperSport. "I thought I would put the boots on and try to help the team really."

For his first time facing the All Blacks, he talked to New Zealand assistant coaches Tana Umaga and Tamati Ellison on Monday about replying to the All Blacks' haka.

"Out of respect for our team and on behalf of myself and my family, I thought it was the right thing to do, to answer the boys and the All Blacks," Nonu said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

So after lining up for the anthems, then watching the haka, he stood alone with the Sharks arrayed behind him, and the All Blacks lined up on the other side of halfway. He performed the All Blacks' own haka, Kapa o Pango, to initial silence from the crowd and growing cheers.

Afterward, he nodded to the All Blacks, many of whom nodded back. Only Codie Taylor and Beauden Barrett still play for New Zealand from Nonu's last squad.

"It was such a privilege and an honour, and to do the haka, showing my respect on behalf of my family to the team I love," Nonu said.

He got into the game with a quarter to go. His first touch was to clatter into flyhalf Ruben Love, who was 2 years old when Nonu debuted for New Zealand.

"I got 20 minutes. I tried my best. It was great to see the [New Zealand] boys," he said.

"The All Blacks opened up in the last 30 minutes and I was chasing my tail. Credit to them, they're improving, and all the best to the brothers for the next game."

AP

World.title: Male redback's bizarre death somersault during sex is in its genes
World.content:
Male redback spiders live fast and die young, ending their lives in a gory ritual of sexual cannibalism.

Female spiders eat their male partners while they mate, and males appear to encourage this behaviour, with their final act being a dramatic somersault onto the female's jaws.

A new study, published in Biology Letters, has pointed to a genetic source for this behaviour.

Male redbacks are less than half the size of their female counterparts, and don't produce venom. (iNatualist: mossylemon/Redback Spider/CC BY 4.0)

The researchers compared the activity of the Australian redback to its close, but non-cannibalistic cousin, New Zealand's katipō.

By breeding the two species together, the researchers, who are based at the University of Hamburg in Germany, learned more about the DNA behind the self-sacrificing somersault.

Bruno Alves Buzatto, a behavioural ecologist at Flinders University who wasn't involved in the research, said the findings were "very striking".

"It supports the idea that being killed during copulation and cannibalised can actually lead to the male's advantage," Dr Buzatto said.

The self-sacrificial redback backflip

Loading...

Redback spiders (Latrodectus hasseltii) are "monogynous": meaning male spiders mate with only one female over their lifetime.

This mating ritual is quite intricate, featuring a "somersault" so that the males' large abdomens are right next to the females' fangs for ease of biting.

Then, the male redbacks constrict their abdomens, which makes them look like they're being squeezed, so they can cheat death for long as possible.

The secret sex lives of redback spiders have been documented for decades, including research by scientists at the University of Toronto seen in the video from ABC TV's Catalyst program in 2010:

Loading...

Dr Buzatto said the self-sacrificing death dance gave males an evolutionary advantage: it improved their chances of offspring.

"The process of being cannibalised increases the time that they mate with the female. Being able to transfer more sperm to the female's spermatheca, which is the organ that the females use to store sperm, provides an advantage."

Female redbacks can store sperm and use it to lay eggs for up to two years after mating.

The katipō (Latrodectus hasseltii), a venomous spider native to New Zealand, is very closely related to the redback.

Katipō have been in decline in New Zealand, and are now difficult to find. (iNaturalist: arnim/Katipō/CC-BY-4.0)

But katipō spiders don't engage in this cannibalistic mating ritual. Instead, males and females tend to mate with each other multiple times.

Cor Vink, an entomologist at Lincoln University in New Zealand who assisted with the study, said katipō evolved from redback spiders about 100,000–200,000 years ago: a blink of an eye in evolutionary terms.

"In that small amount of time, that whole behaviour is lost," Dr Vink said.

"It's really interesting when behaviours like that can be lost. We don't know enough about how behaviours are coded in the DNA of invertebrates."

Cross-breeding spiders to test genetics

The researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together to see how mating behaviours were displayed in their offspring.

Dr Vink collected both species of spider from different sites in New Zealand, where the redback spider is an invasive species.

"We collected adult redbacks and then fed them up, took them back, grabbed their egg sacks and then they got sent to Germany. We did the same thing with the katipō as well," he said.

No-one has died from a redback bite since the introduction of antivenom in the 1960s. (iNatualist: prissm/Redback Spider/CC BY 4.0)

Both redbacks and katipō bites can require antivenom, but there haven’t been any recorded deaths in decades (for redbacks) or centuries (for katipō).

Dr Vink said both spider species were "shy and retiring", but he and his fellow collectors wore gloves as an extra precaution.

"When they bite you, you won't die, you'll just feel like you're going to," Dr Vink said.

"It's a pretty horrible experience from what I've been told and I'm not willing to find out what it's like."

Once the spider eggs had made it to Germany, the researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together and reared male hybrids to maturity.

Then, they added the hybrids to webs built by, and housing, female katipō, filming their behaviour with infrared cameras.

Katipō (pictured) and redback spiders are both related to black widow spiders, which are found in the Americas. (iNaturalist: arnim/Katipō/CC-BY-4.0)

They analysed the footage from 104 mating rituals, looking for signs of both the somersault trick and the abdominal constriction.

Roughly half the hybrids performed the life-ending somersault while mating.

Because of the way they'd bred male redbacks with female katipō, this 50/50 split allowed the researchers to conclude the somersault trait was inherited on a spider sex chromosome.

But the other behaviour — the abdominal wiggle — wasn't displayed as clearly, suggesting the genetics for this trait were more complicated.

The researchers observed the spiders (a) somersaulting, (b) squeezing their abdomens, or (c) doing neither of these things while mating. (Supplied: Uludag, Ivanov, Krehenwinkel, Schneider, 2026, Biology Letters, doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2026.0211, CC-BY 4.0)

This surprised the researchers, who were expecting both traits to have a common genetic source.

Michael Kasumovic, an evolutionary biologist at the University of New South Wales who wasn't involved in the research, said this was a neat finding.

"Given how important both traits are to survival, we would guess that they should be strongly linked together. But they aren't, and that suggests they evolved independently. And that's really cool," he said.

"This study highlights that maybe we need to think about how different species interact and how that can lead to new traits evolving and new species appearing."

Dr Buzatto said he wasn't surprised by the study's findings.

" We know that a lot of very complex behaviours can be encoded by some fairly simple genetic basis. "

But he said spider sex chromosomes were very complicated, and differed from species to species, meaning there was still much to learn.

"I feel like the more we look, the more weird and surprising things we'll find with spiders," Dr Buzatto said.

"We've probably only described and documented a quarter of the spiders that exist, maybe a third, we're not too sure … That really opens people's minds to why we find all these crazy, unusual, surprising behaviours and life histories in these animals."

Genetic research to conserve NZ's spiders

Dr Vink said this genetic research could help to protect the katipō, which is in decline in New Zealand — in part because of the redback spider.

In New Zealand, redback spiders are predating on and threatening several native species like skinks and beetles.

But the biggest threat to the rare katipō is that the two spiders can interbreed and create hybrids.

"In New Zealand, we have a very real danger of losing a species through hybridisation," Dr Vink said.

In his own research, Dr Vink is studying redback spider pheromones to see if they can be used to control populations.

"The idea is that if we can attract enough males using the pheromone, we can reduce the male population, which will crash the overall population because males can only mate once," he said.

Research into courtship and genetics can help with this conservation technique, alongside giving researchers more data to track katipō and redback populations.

World.title: History beckons for Phil Sami after the hard life of a Gold Coast hero
World.content:
As the weather gets warmer and the dreams of the NRL's elite become all the more real, the competition strugglers begin the march towards the end.

If South Sydney defeats Canterbury on Friday night the ninth-placed Bulldogs will be two wins outside the top eight with just three rounds remaining and their play-off hopes will feel more mathematical than truly possible.

It means, with the top eight all bust set in stone, the nine clubs who will miss out on the finals in 2026 face four matches with uncertain stakes.

Careers will begin for the young as some look to the future and end for the old as others celebrate the past on their way out the door.

Tedious debates about a potential wildcard round or expanded finals series, where games are called "content" as they transform into mere vessels for revenue, will be reheated.

Spoiling the dreams of their betters becomes the greatest prize a struggling team can hope for and incessant mentions of how one side or another is only "playing for pride" will instead merely compound their shame.

Sami has been one of Gold Coast's best during some of the club's hardest times. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It is amidst this wreckage that Phillip Sami, who has lived the hard life of a Gold Coast legend, will try and make history.

Sami is currently level with Anthony Don as the Titans all-time leading try-scorer with 85 and he has four games to land one more and leave for St George Illawarra at season's end as the top dog.

It would be a just reward for a decade spent fighting for a cause that seems to be perpetually starting over.

Counting interims, Sami has played under nine head coaches in his 10 seasons with Gold Coast.

He's played in just one semi-final, which doubles as the Titans only finals match since 2010, and has never played on a team with a winning record.

Sami debuted for Gold Coast back in 2017. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

He has been through it, as anybody who sticks around long enough to hold a Gold Coast record must, which means he knows these curious final weeks of the season very well.

Expect more of his best because if the lure of premierships was all that drove Sami he would have shot through long ago and he wouldn't be here now, on the verge of claiming the record.

A cynic might say it's a modest piece of history. Of all the clubs that have existed for as long as the Titans have or more, only Western Suburbs Magpies have a lower total for their top try-scorer.

But only a snob turns up their nose when a house record is concerned and given Gold Coast always have to fight to make themselves heard, Sami has done more for that fight than most.

He's chased this record the hard way. Given the club's point-scoring struggles and playmaker upheaval over the years, sparkling backline efforts have rarely been easy to find and there are precious few catch and fall efforts to be found here.

But every now and then, Sami goes big-game hunting and when he does he seems to have a special talent for winning battles using the weapons of his enemies.

One of the first times he showed this quality was in 2018 against the Warriors when Samis scored what remains his greatest try.

In those days, getting a hand on the light-stepping Roger Tuivasa-Sheck was like catching smoke and Sami, in just his second year of first grade, didn't so much give that year's Dally M medallist a taste of his own medicine but a lethal overdose.

Sami did the same when he flew over Clint Gutherson during the days when Parramatta really was the latter's kingdom before hitting him with his own celebration dance.

He showed he's not lost his touch earlier this season when he rounded Reece Walsh en route to a 70-metre solo effort that left the prince of Brisbane grasping at ghosts as Sami howled like a wolf.

It's not just with tries or even with football — Sami has a rare gift for being larger than life.

When he played two matches for Queensland back in 2020 a coach from his schoolboy days detailed the time Sami outran a kangaroo during a match.

It sounds like something from a folk song but rap is more Sami's speed given Goodna rapper Lisi shouted him out on a track later that same year.

At the time he was best known for the step on Tuivasa-Sheck and the moment he ran down ran down Josh Addo-Carr, which came at a time when that was like shooting Jesse James.

That try-saver, like his all-round play this year, is proof there's more to his game than just the fun stuff.

Sami has run more metres than any other player in the league, over 200 more than second place and 500 more than the next best winger. He's averaging 218 metres gained per game, the best mark of his career by miles.

He's also top when it comes to post-contact metres, a full 400 metres ahead of any other flanker, and teammate Keano Kini is the only player in the whole NRL who's run the ball more times.

Throw in that Sami only needs one more line break and one more try will match his career-best total for a single season in both categories and you can make a hipster's case he's a shot for one of the wing spots in the Dally M team of the year, making his progress towards the record an even more furious charge.

He has given his absolute best in service of one last fresh start for the Titans and perhaps this will even be the one that sticks.

Gold Coast fans have plenty to be optimistic about in the years to come. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

In Kini, Jayden Campebll, Zane Harrison and Oliver Pascoe, Gold Coast have a spine of playmakers that feels full of exciting possibilities.

Josh Hannay has shown some promising signs as coach, displaying a sharp eye for the kind of fighters the Titans will need in the years to come.

One more win will give them more victories than last year and they're a chance of finishing above Brisbane for just the sixth time in their history.

In a broader sense, after two decades the club has found a lived-in quality by sitting more comfortably with it's own history as an enticing future beckons.

Why Gold Coast has already won Magic Round One of the best parts of Magic Round is going jersey-spotting but before a ball is kicked in Brisbane the Titans have already cleaned up via their Chargers-inspired retro strip.

Sami will not be on hand to see it. He's taken up a three-year deal with St George Illawarra, one which was too good to refuse even as the Titans were open to keeping him.

So he has four games left to get one last try. The first chance is against Newcastle on Sunday and it won't be easy.

The Knights have defied their bulging casualty ward in recent weeks to keep themselves in the race for the top four and will be warm favourites at home.

But Sami has never had it easy and no Titan ever really does, so why should the moment of achievement for club and player be any different?

They've lived through dark days together, enough for both know it's how to take the shiny moments where you find them, regardless of how and when they come.

When you are in the final days of a lost year a player can either accept that fate or try and change it on the hope that this game can be better than the last just because it's a fresh start.

Sami has spent his career believing that and proving it with his actions. He wouldn't have scored these tries and lasted this long if he didn't.

Now he has a chance at a prize all his own, that he has fought for his own way and if he can break the record before leaving it will mark his ultimate reward — to live as a Gold Coast hero.

That title tells the tale of a hard footballing life but someone had to live it and Sami has lived it all the way.

World.title: The Office star Lucy Davis announces she has incurable cancer
World.content:
Actress Lucy Davis, best known for her role as Dawn Tinsley on the UK version of The Office, has announced she has "incurable" stage 4 breast cancer.

In a post on Instagram, Davis revealed she had been diagnosed one-and-a-half years ago and the cancer had metastasised to her bones including her spine, right hip and ribs.

"The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo," Davis said.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn't bother getting it checked.

"So I guess I'm saying don't ignore anything — get everything checked out."

According to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, breast cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia, after prostate cancer, with more than 20,000 people in Australia diagnosed every year.

Lucy Davis read out the Ring the Bell poem in her Instagram post. (Instagram: reallucydavis)

Stage 4 breast cancer, sometimes known as metastatic or advanced breast cancer, is when the disease has spread to other parts of the body. There is currently no cure; however, treatment is available to manage the illness and extend life.

Davis, who has also starred in Shaun of the Dead, Wonder Woman and The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, said she was now trying bring as much fun into the rest of her life as possible.

"I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there's a lot I have learned from it, and I'm grateful for that," she said.

In the post, Davis reads out the poem Ring the Bell, which is traditionally read after a patient completes chemotherapy or radiation treatment and rings a bell just once instead of the usual three times.

She described the pain she is in and said she would sometimes need to use a wheelchair.

"The thing that has been most vital to me is humour," Davis said.

"I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they're really good at), and most importantly of all to not treat me like a sick person.

" There's nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you're unwell. "

She said she was not scared of what was next and she planned to continue her work for animal rights.

Davis is a long-term vegan and a vocal animal activist. In 2007, she posed nude for PETA's campaign against the Guards Division's continued use of traditional bearskin caps.

The Office co-star Ricky Gervais left a heart comment on Davis's post.

"For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well," she wrote.

"Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose."

World.title: The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCancer The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis Kayla Olaya Updated August 12, 2026 — 9:59am ,first published 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star of the UK version of The Office Lucy Davis has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer but is “not scared of whatever comes next”. The 53-year-old who played Dawn Tinsley, Martin Freeman’s character’s love interest in the show, shared the update on Instagram early on Wednesday (AEST) after being diagnosed with cancer a year and a half ago. She said it had now metastasised in her bones, making it too late for chemotherapy. Lucy Davis (middle right) pictured with the main cast of BBC’s The Office - Mackenzie Crook, left, Ricky Gervais, middle left, and Martin Warning. BBC “A year and a half ago I was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer, which has metastasised to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo,” Davis said in the caption to her post. “As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.



“I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her dog, which died in 2024] sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me.” In the video post, Davis rings the bell – a ceremony for cancer patients marking the end of treatment – to applause. In the caption, she urges readers not to ignore small lumps or signs as she had. “The initial lump that I felt wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out,” Davis said. Davis, who also had roles in the Wonder Woman films and the comic zombie horror Sean of the Dead, said that as her pain intensified, tasks such as standing or walking could become difficult and told her followers to expect to see her in a wheelchair from time to time.



Lucy Davis has shared that she’s been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer. UK Press via Getty Images “If you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push,” she joked, adding that humour has been “vital” to her throughout this journey. “I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at, and most importantly of all, to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she said. In her post, Davis said that despite her pain and diagnosis, she would continue to pursue her activism for animal rights and continue to work. “I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life,” she wrote.



Jenna Fischer, who played Pam Beesly, the equivalent of Davis’s character Dawn in the US version of The Office, commented below the post supporting her decision to work with cancer. “Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let’s spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort,” Fischer said. Fischer was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023, but following treatment, she announced that she was cancer-free in late 2024. Davis signed off her post to fellow cancer battlers, sing that: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally”. “We all get to do it however we choose.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Ex-girlfriend of complainant ‘J’ set to give evidence as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. I will be bringing you the latest from court today along with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete known as “J”, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. KATE GERAGHTY

Yesterday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what he had told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy. Her evidence continues today.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.
