World.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage from the Independent Commission Against Corruption.

I’m state political reporter Jessica McSweeney, and along with a team of the Sydney Morning Herald’s senior writers, we’ll be bringing you all the latest news as it happens. Today we’re expecting to hear more evidence from lobbyist and political operator Jeremy Greenwood.

Before evidence begins at 10am, let’s take a look at what we covered yesterday:

Jeremy Greenwood conceded that he commissioned a “shit sheet” on then-police minister David Elliott in a bid to discredit the former MP. One of Greenwood’s clients was the disgraced developer Jean Nassif, who is known to hate Elliott, but the lobbyist insisted the dirt sheet was done to defend Greenwood’s business.

Commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, was clearly growing frustrated with Greenwood’s answers and asked the lobbyist if he had trouble understanding English words. Greenwood said he did not.

Greenwood said he would do anything for his friend Jean-Claude Perrottet, including giving him money from his business account, and repeatedly said he could not recall any payments coming from hotelier Michael O’Hara, who had agreed to financially support the Reformers.

The commission also heard that Greenwood took a 6am call from his friend and former business partner Christian Ellis on Tuesday, just hours after giving his first day of evidence. Greenwood said the call was over the encrypted app Signal and was just a welfare check. Ellis is also a person of interest in this inquiry but now lives in the United Kingdom and is refusing to give evidence.

You can watch the ICAC’s livestream here.

World.title: Island hotel in a stopover favourite is an unsurprising hit with Aussies
World.content:
★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews Island hotel in a stopover favourite is an unsurprising hit with Aussies Craig Platt August 12, 2026 — 8:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The place The Village Sentosa, Singapore The pools are the centrepiece of the property. Kids can fill out their own check-in forms in the lobby. Check-in



Located on Singapore’s island of fun, Sentosa, The Village is part of a precinct of four hotels by Far East Hospitality, each with a different focus. The Outpost is a sophisticated, adults-only space with a rooftop bar and pool, Oasia is wellness focused, while the Barracks, inside a former Singapore military barracks, offers a luxurious stay in a heritage setting. The Village, meanwhile, is squarely aimed at families, which is apparent from the outset where a small set of steps allow little ones to stand up at the reception desk and complete their own check-in forms. It’s also popular with Australians, who make up one quarter of all guests. 



Family rooms are two rooms joined together. Rooms are compact at just 22 square metres for a Superior room, while a Deluxe room is just four square metres larger (the only noticeable difference is the inclusion of a chaise longue next to the bed). Like many modern hotels, there’s no bathroom as such, with a shower and toilet off the entryway, with storage and a sink on the other side. That said, there is, at least, a heavy sliding door that can be closed to separate the entry and the bed area to provide some privacy. There’s no desk, but a shelf in front of the bed folds out so you can sit on the end of the bed to use it like one. I’m travelling with my partner and two kids, so we’re in a “Deluxe Family room”, which is two Deluxe rooms connected through a door. There are some nice kid-friendly touches, like activity packs and mini-bathrobes. The natural timber look and bright colours offer summer vibes and give the rooms a sunny, airy, feel despite the compact space. Rather than provide tea and coffee in the room, there’s a “Village Hub” on each floor. As someone who often uses up all the tea bags in the room before they get replenished by housekeeping, I’m a fan of being able to help myself. The food Native Kitchen. Across the four properties there’s a wide range of restaurants, covering a wide variety of cuisines from traditional Chinese to French and Eurasian fusion. Native Kitchen is The Village’s restaurant, specialising in local Singaporean favourites (though with a few Western dishes on the menu too) including Hainanese chicken rice, nasi lemak and laksa (though you’ll pay much more than you would in a hawker centre or food court on the main island). There’s also a takeaway food counter in the lobby for quick snacks like sandwiches and pastries.



Stepping out The Wings of Time show is surprisingly impressive. Craig Platt There are plenty of things for families to do on Sentosa, both free and ticketed. I admit I’m a little dubious about attending The Wings of Time show – the updated version of the musical fountains that have been an attraction on Sentosa for decades (and first seen by myself back in 1997). But the modern version of the musical fountain, moved to the beach and using pyrotechnics, projections and lasers to tell its simple story, is great fun and undeniably impressive. At just 20 minutes long, it’s also the perfect length to hold the attention of younger kids. Our kids also love the Sentosa Cable Car, which has a station a short distance from the hotel. We ride at dusk and watch the sun set over the bay. The verdict The variety of pools will keep the whole family entertained for hours.



While you’re some distance away from the highlights of central Singapore, if you’re looking for somewhere to unwind during a stopover that the whole family can enjoy, The Village is a good bet. Essentials Rooms at The Village Sentosa start from $S370 ($410) a night. See villagehotels.asia Our rating out of five ★★★½

World.title: The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCancer The Office star Lucy Davis reveals ‘incurable’ cancer diagnosis Kayla Olaya Updated August 12, 2026 — 9:59am ,first published 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Star of the UK version of The Office Lucy Davis has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer but is “not scared of whatever comes next”. The 53-year-old who played Dawn Tinsley, Martin Freeman’s character’s love interest in the show, shared the update on Instagram early on Wednesday (AEST) after being diagnosed with cancer a year and a half ago. She said it had now metastasised in her bones, making it too late for chemotherapy. Lucy Davis (middle right) pictured with the main cast of BBC’s The Office - Mackenzie Crook, left, Ricky Gervais, middle left, and Martin Warning. BBC “A year and a half ago I was diagnosed with stage four breast cancer, which has metastasised to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo,” Davis said in the caption to her post. “As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.



“I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her dog, which died in 2024] sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me.” In the video post, Davis rings the bell – a ceremony for cancer patients marking the end of treatment – to applause. In the caption, she urges readers not to ignore small lumps or signs as she had. “The initial lump that I felt wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out,” Davis said. Davis, who also had roles in the Wonder Woman films and the comic zombie horror Sean of the Dead, said that as her pain intensified, tasks such as standing or walking could become difficult and told her followers to expect to see her in a wheelchair from time to time.



Lucy Davis has shared that she’s been diagnosed with incurable stage four breast cancer. UK Press via Getty Images “If you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push,” she joked, adding that humour has been “vital” to her throughout this journey. “I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at, and most importantly of all, to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell,” she said. In her post, Davis said that despite her pain and diagnosis, she would continue to pursue her activism for animal rights and continue to work. “I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life,” she wrote.



Jenna Fischer, who played Pam Beesly, the equivalent of Davis’s character Dawn in the US version of The Office, commented below the post supporting her decision to work with cancer. “Beautiful post. Love you lots. And yes to working with cancer! Let’s spread that message far and wide! How working is such a comfort,” Fischer said. Fischer was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2023, but following treatment, she announced that she was cancer-free in late 2024. Davis signed off her post to fellow cancer battlers, sing that: “For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally”. “We all get to do it however we choose.” Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Ex-girlfriend of complainant ‘J’ set to give evidence as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. I will be bringing you the latest from court today along with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete known as “J”, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. KATE GERAGHTY

Yesterday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what he had told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy. Her evidence continues today.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Yellow rain watches issued for Northland, Auckland and Westland
World.content:
Northern and eastern areas of Northland and Auckland north of Orewa are under a heavy rain watch on Wednesday.

The watches which also cover Great Barrier Island came into effect at 10am, MetService says.

A low-pressure system southwest of New Zealand is driving a frontal band of rain eastwards, mainly affecting the top half of the North Island and Westland today.

The forecast which applies for the upper North Island through to 1am on Thursday is for periods of rain with some heavy falls, and the amounts may approach the criteria for an upgrade to a warning.

The rain will ease from the north on Wednesday afternoon and evening, MetService says.

Meanwhile, in the South Island, there will be periods of heavy rain from 2pm today through until 6am tomorrow in Westland.

The rainfall may be especially heavy about the ranges.

The band of rain has made its way to Aotearoa from the Tasman Sea and might result in rain and showers for most of the North Island on Thursday.

World.title: Kiwi ICE detainee Everlee Wihongi on 'dehumanising conditions' in custody
World.content:
What gives you hope when you're being held in a US immigration detention facility?

For New Zealand citizen Everlee Wihongi, it was the support of her family and loved ones, but she says hope can be a bad thing in a place like that.

"Lots of times it was bad to have hope that things would go well," she said.

"It was like I can't look too far into the future because I don't know how long I'll be here."

Wihongi, who has lived in the US for decades and holds a green card, was detained by ICE in early April after coming back from New Zealand.

She was held for more than 70 days because of a 2016 cannabis conviction that was later thrown out by the courts.

Now, she's back home in Wisconsin with her family.

Speaking to RNZ, Wihongi said her time in detainment was one of the most miserable experiences of her entire existence.

Officials at the facility would refer to her as a bunk-bed number, rather than by her name, she said.

She wasn't Everlee Wihongi, she was 'Six Up'.

"It was dehumanising conditions," Wihongi said.

"Whenever you'd have an appointment or you had to go see a lawyer, anything, they would just go 'Six Up, you have an appointment'."

Wihongi said meal times at the facilities she was held in were another challenge.

"The first spot I was in, we had to get up at 6am to eat, and if you didn't get up for breakfast and you didn't eat," she said.

"When I was in Arizona, you had to get up at 3.45am to get breakfast, and if you didn't go, then you just didn't eat till lunchtime, which is around 1pm."

Wihongi was first held in an ICE facility in California, before being moved to Arizona and spending a night on the floor in a Texan holding facility along the way.

In transit, Wihongi described seeing other detainees being removed from a plane before they could board.

She and others had been woken at 1.30 that morning, shackled, and moved out, but weren't on the plane until later that evening.

"We could see the people coming off the plane, but they couldn't see into the van," she said.

"There were children in shackles, a pregnant lady, old people, everybody just being marched around like herded animals really, getting off the plane, getting into these other buses."

The conviction that saw Wihongi detained by ICE in the first place was thrown out by a court in June.

She described the moment as unbelievable.

"I didn't want to be too excited or get too ahead of myself," she said.

"I thought for sure it'd be a few more months they would try and hold me in there, I didn't think that they were going to let me out right away."

Wihongi said having hope in detention meant you'd be devastated at one point or another.

Everlee Wihongi and whanau Supplied / Courtney Wihongi

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade had been providing consular assistance during Wihongi's detainment. She said staff from the New Zealand's Los Angeles consulate were helpful, evening bringing her New Zealand chocolate on one visit.

Staff helped her recover documents like her passport, Green Card, and drivers license - something she didn't have when she was released.

Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters had said Wihongi was detained for not declaring her historic cannabis possession conviction, but that was completely false, she said.

"In all my time coming back and forth, I've never been given one of those forms."

"Even when the consulate asked, 'did you get one of those papers to mark your conviction?' I was never given one of those," Wihongi said.

She was shocked by the public response to her time in ICE custody.

"It was something else to come out of something like that to so much love and support from not only my family, but strangers and people I didn't know."

She hoped those still detained by ICE had the same love and support she experienced.

"There are just more people in there that have nothing, they don't have the family support like I did, they don't have their country supporting them like I did, I just wish more people could experience that," Wihongi said.

World.title: Pacific media figures pay tribute to Solomons legend George Atkin
World.content:
Tributes have flowed in for the renowned Solomon Islands journalist, George Atkin, who has died.

As well as being a former correspondent for the then-RNZ International, Atkin was a leading figure in journalism in Solomon Islands and in the Pacific Islands region.

He was the first President of the Media Association of Solomon Islands, serving from 1985 to 1989 and was a respected member of the country's media fraternity.

The veteran journalist worked for numerous mainstream media outlets such as the Solomon Star newspaper, Island Sun newspaper and the Solomon Islands Broadcasting Corporation.

A prominent Solomon islands media figure, Robert Iroga, said Atkin was an editor, journalist, storyteller and mentor who understood the power of the pen.

"He understood that journalism was not simply about filling pages or broadcasting news. He understood that words could change policies, challenge governments, expose wrongdoing and even force leaders to resign."

Some of the region's best known names in the news media sector have also paid tribute to Atkin on social media.

Alexander Rheeney, a former editor of both PNG's Post Courier newspaper and the Samoa Observer, said Atkin "was a legend and well respected by the media fraternity and the public".

TVNZ's long-time Pacific correspondent Barbara Dreaver said Atkin "leaves a legacy that will be remembered".

RNZ Pacific manager Moera Tuilaepa-Taylor said that Atkin "was a true professional and understood all the complex layers of politics in his country".

World.title: Ex-cops not guilty of obstructing justice relating to Alan Hall case
World.content:
Two former police officers accused of obstructing justice in an investigation which led to the wrongful conviction of Alan Hall in the 1980s have been found not guilty.

The men, whose names are suppressed, have been on trial in the High Court at Auckland charged with wilfully attempting to obstruct, prevent, pervert or defeat the course of justice.

A third former defendant has since died.

Justice Ian Gault delivered the decision on Wednesday morning. The men's interim name suppression is extended while the court considers an application for permanent name suppression.

Arthur Easton. Supplied / Police

Hall spent 17 years in prison after being convicted of murdering Arthur Easton, who was killed during a home invasion by a man wielding a bayonet.

World.title: Litigation costs a factor as ASB net profit drops to $1.3b
World.content:
ASB's full-year profit has dipped slightly due to litigation costs, but home and commercial lending increased.

Financial results for the year ended June versus the year before.

Cash net profit after tax: NZ$1.318 billion, down 2%

Net interest income: NZ$3.14 billion, up 8%

Total operating income: NZ$3.55 billion, up 6%

Operating expenses: NZ$1.65 billion, up 16%

Home lending: NZ$84.5 billion, up 6%

Business and rural lending: NZ$36.2 billion, up 6%

ASB has reported a full-year profit of NZ$1.3 billion, down 2 percent on the previous year due to higher operating costs, including a $135 million class action settlement.

ASB, which is owned by the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, is the first of the big four Australian-owned banks to report its New Zealand result.

Operating costs were up 16 percent to NZ$1.65b.

ASB said this was due to higher staff costs, the class action settlement, spending on technology, and increased provisions for bad debts, which rose 30 percent to NZ$78m.

Its net interest margin increased by three basis points to 2.3 percent.

Home lending rose 6 percent to $84.5b, while business and rural lending increased 6 percent to $36.2b.

Commenting on the result, ASB chief executive Vittoria Shortt said it had been a challenging year given the economic disruption caused by the conflict in the Middle East and rising inflation.

"The economic recovery has been very stop-start. Although we had momentum at the beginning of the financial year, it's been a very different second half.

"The conflict in the Middle East and subsequent global oil price shock have caused significant disruption, changing the inflation outlook and pushing interest rates up faster than anticipated."

However, Shortt said ASB customers had weathered the storm well, with fewer households experiencing difficulties repaying loans.

"While we expect economic momentum to return in the coming months, uncertainty remains the new norm and we're cognisant that many New Zealanders will continue to face cost pressures.

World.title: Fiji corrections officer charged over alleged assault of Australian prisoner
World.content:
One of seven Fiji corrections officers alleged to have been involved in the assault of an Australian citizen at the Lautoka Remand Centre has been charged.

The Corrections Service suspended all seven officers last week, after a video depicting a brutal assault of a prisoner by officers in Lautoka went viral on Fijian social media.

The incident occurred on June 14th, according to the timestamp in the footage.

One of the officers, Asaeli Sorovaki, appeared in court on assault charges on Monday. He was granted bail with his case adjourned to September 7th, according to Fiji Village.

The others have yet to see their day in court.

It's also been revealed that the remand prisoner allegedly beaten by the officers is an Australian citizen.

In a statement on its Facebook page, Corrections said the prisoner had been medically examined and remained stable in custody.

Lautoka's Natabua Corrections Centre. Fiji Govt

"Meanwhile, the six officers who remain suspended allegedly for breaches relating to the standard operating procedures and lawful instructions in the course of their duties and which are linked to the reported incident will await internal disciplinary proceedings to be heard by the designated Tribunal," Corrections said.

World.title: Red Fox Tavern murder: Pair whose convictions were quashed seek costs from Crown
World.content:
Two men, whose convictions for the 1987 Red Fox Tavern murder were overturned by the Supreme Court last month, are seeking costs from the Crown.

Publican Chris Bush was fatally shot at the Maramarua pub and two balaclava-clad offenders fled with more $30,000.

The case went unsolved for almost 30 years before James Wilson and Mark Hoggart were charged and subsequently convicted in 2021.

Chris Bush Supplied / NZ Police

Last month, the Supreme Court acquitted the pair after deliberating two years, finding there was no reliable evidence to prove they were at the scene of the crime.

Lawyers for Wilson and Hoggart had earlier failed in their bid to overturn their convictions at the Court of Appeal.

On Wednesday morning, the case was called in an administrative hearing at the High Court in Auckland.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki child-safety IT overhaul passes milestone
World.content:
Oranga Tamariki has got Cabinet approval for detailed plans for a long-awaited $68m replacement of old information systems that slow down how it safeguards children.

This comes three years after the project got the previous government's nod amid warnings the 25-year-old case management system was increasingly unreliable. But in 2024 it had to be reset, as RNZ revealed.

Since then notifications by the public of children at risk have surged while months of planning the upgrade have slipped by.

The information systems record sensitive and private information about the lives of children.

Over a year ago Oranga Tamariki told RNZ it had delayed a review of its detailed business case to "get the maximum value".

This week the ministry said Cabinet recently approved the business case and it expected to sign a contract to design the system next month.

A review in March rated the project 'amber-green'.

"This rating indicates that successful delivery is likely, although continued management attention is required to ensure identified risks are effectively managed," chief social worker Nicolette Dickson said in a statement.

Since it got funding in Budget 2024, Oranga Tamariki had gone looking for the best case management platform and this search was now nearing completion, she said.

It had aligned the project with the government's new 'Digital Target State' introduced in December 2025 to make savings and link up public sector IT work.

"We have gained a number of insights, including from overseas child protection jurisdictions who have completed similar case management system changes, about how to ensure cost-effective, timely and quality implementation."

A Cabinet paper in 2024 said none of the three main benefits of the systems overhaul "can be fully realised until the completion of the programme". Those three included improved safety for tamariki, reduced harm from youth offending and better support for OT staff.

Getting the right tech was expected to be "realistic and achievable" back then.

Dickson said the project had several independent quality control mechanisms in place.

The $68m covers only the first phase and other Budgets were going to be called on for later funding.

"Oranga Tamariki is unable to fund further programme costs without impacting the services it provides to children," the 2024 Cabinet paper stated.

This project is meant to dovetail in with the Ministry of Social Development's big service upgrade programme, Te Pae Tawhiti. The first stage of that was on time and on budget, according to a Treasury paper in late 2025. The second and third parts run from now till 2032

Budget 2026 had $180m for Oranga Tamariki to improve responses to children but did not mention technology as part of that.

Dickson said the ministry had also since 2024 made a small number of improvements to its old tech, as well as to social worker practice.

In May it launched a new digital tool called All About Me used to make 1000 care plans since. This comes two years after talk of a prototype.

World.title: Trump says FIFA would be making 'terrible mistake' to remove Infantino
World.content:
Embattled FIFA leader Gianni Infantino has a powerful and vocal supporter — US President Donald Trump.

As football organisations around the world continue to call for the resignation of the FIFA president, post-World Cup, Trump blasted that idea in a message he posted to Truth Social on Monday night.

"FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino," Trump wrote.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!"

UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North America, Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) banded together earlier in the week to release an open letter, signed by the president and general secretary of each organisation, urging Infantino's resignation.

Infantino has been under fire since last month's failed plan to launch the FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would have sold part of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors to raise billions of dollars.

He apparently caused further damage by holding a crisis meeting last week in Morocco with some members of FIFA's management team.

Trump is a close ally of Infantino's after the FIFA boss awarded him the FIFA Peace Prize. (Getty Images: Kevin Dietsch)

"This recent meeting, where a select number of members of the FIFA Management Committee — not the full Committee — were summoned abroad, rather than leadership going to Zurich to address the heart of FIFA, its staff, only reinforces these concerns and represents a continuation of the very pattern of conduct that brought us to this moment," reads the letter from UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Also Monday, US Soccer and others issued their own statement backing CONCACAF.

"US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU (Caribbean Football Union) and UNCAF (Central American Football Union) stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens FIFA's governance, transparency and accountability," the statement read.

Infantino, 56, has served as FIFA president since his initial election on February 26, 2016. His current term runs through 2027, and he has announced his bid for re-election to extend his tenure to 2031.

Reuters

World.title: Wallaroos name new head coach as 2029 Rugby World Cup looms on horizon
World.content:
The Wallaroos have made another key appointment in the build-up to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup with Sione Fukofuka named head coach.

Fukofuka will begin the role in 2027 after the Wallaroos become a full-time program.

He will work under Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, who took on his newly created position last month.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Fukofuka was Scotland women's head coach until last week.

He was granted a release from his contract for family and personal reasons.

The 47-year-old will be returning home to Australia, having begun his coaching career while working as a teacher in the Queensland schools system.

He previously served as an assistant on the Wallaroos staff and was USA head coach between 2023-25.

"Although a difficult decision to leave the Scottish role, this opportunity allows me to be in Sydney closer to my family," Fukofuka said in an RA statement.

"I know many of the players and coaches well from my time in the Queensland and Australian systems and, as we transition to a full-time program this year, the opportunity for growth is enormous."

The Wallaroos' on-field results will improve once the program goes full-time. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

RA is determined the Wallaroos make an impression at the next Women's Rugby World Cup, which Australia will host.

They departed last year's tournament at the quarterfinal stage and are ranked ninth in the world.

The Wallaroos went winless during April's Pacific Four Series following losses to Canada (24-0), USA (33-12) and New Zealand (40-5).

But the move to full-time status will be a game changer for the Wallaroos in terms of improving on-field results.

The alignment of the Wallaroos and Australian sevens programs, under Walsh's guidance, will also make the squad competitive with the likes of New Zealand and reigning world champions England.

Walsh said he was confident the Wallaroos would make progress under Fukofuka, whose contract runs through until the end of the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"Sione is a pioneer among international coaches of Pasifika heritage and a proud product of the Australian rugby coaching system," Walsh said.

"He is highly regarded by players and staff alike for his connection, team culture and driving high standards within the daily training environment.

"He is well-positioned to lead the Wallaroos into a new era and a generational opportunity presented by the home Rugby World Cup in 2029."

The Wallaroos still have six Tests to play this year, with a return bout against New Zealand coming up in Auckland on August 22.

The clash with New Zealand has historical significance as it will be the Wallaroos' 100th Test.

They head to Europe next month to play WXV Global Series Tests against England in Salford (September 13), France in Aix-en-Provence (September 20) and Scotland in Edinburgh (September 27).

The Wallaroos will later host Scotland in Sydney (October 17) and Canberra (October 23) as part of the WXV Global Series.

Vast coaching experience

Fukofuka took charge of Scotland last December.

Under his watch, Scotland finished fifth in this year's Women's Six Nations Championship with a 1-4 win-loss record.

Former Wallabies hooker and ACT Brumbies men's coach David Nucifora, now working as Scottish Rugby performance director, said Fukofuka left with the governing body's blessings.

Fukofuka moved to Scotland after stepping down as USA head coach following the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup in England.

Sione Fukofuka coached USA at the 2025 Women's Rugby World Cup. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

USA, which drew 31-31 with the Wallaroos in the pool stage, did not advance to the quarterfinals but Fukofuka was credited with improving the level of professionalism within the Eagles program during his tenure.

"Sione is a leader with a comprehensive knowledge of Australian and international systems and a reputation for creating world-class team environments and standards," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

As Fukofuka will not take the reins until next year, Walsh will oversee the Wallaroos' coaching transition team for the remainder of the Test season.

Walsh recently guided Australia to its World Championship victory in women's sevens, ending a successful second stint as head coach.

He coached Australia to a historic victory at the 2016 Rio Olympics during his first term.

The Wallaroos' coaching transition team includes NSW head coach Mike Ruthven, who led the Waratahs to the Super Rugby Women's title last month, and ex-Wallabies captain Ben Mowen.

Mowen currently works on the Brumbies' coaching staff.

Interim coaches Sam Needs and Gill Bourke have departed the Wallaroos' set-up.

World.title: Fraser confirms intentions for Carlton coaching job after hot streak
World.content:
Carlton caretaker Josh Fraser wants the full-time coaching job.

Fraser has told Carlton hierarchy he is keen to become the permanent head coach after his stunning success as interim boss.

The former Collingwood ruckman has won 10 of 12 games since the departure of Michael Voss and is now among five candidates for the permanent job.

Fraser, 44, initially said he wasn't interested in being the full-time coach from next season.

Carlton has won 10 out of 12 games under Fraser's guidance, surging into finals contention. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

But he has changed his mind after his blistering start to coaching, and now appears the frontrunner in a field of five.

Fremantle's Jaymie Graham, St Kilda's Corey Enright, Geelong's James Kelly — all current assistant coaches — have interviewed for the role, along with Hawthorn's head of development Daniel Giansiracusa.

Fraser's about-turn comes as he revives the on-field fortunes of the Blues, who were languishing with one win and eight losses when Voss departed in mid-May.

Carlton appears set for a wildcard finals berth, sitting 10th on the ladder and two wins clear of 11th-placed St Kilda with two rounds remaining.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Blues meet the Western Bulldogs on Sunday before their last home-and-away game against ladder-leaders Fremantle.

Fraser, who played 200 games with Collingwood and 18 at Gold Coast, began his coaching career as coach of the Suns' state league side.

He then coached Carlton and Collingwood at VFL level before returning to the Blues as an assistant to Voss this season.

Two weeks ago, Carlton's football boss Chris Davies said the club wanted Fraser to apply for the full-time role.

"We think he should put his hand up," Davies said at the time.

Since those comments, Fraser has overseen a 76-point thrashing of reigning premiers Brisbane and a 44-point victory over the Saints.

AAP

World.title: More elite women coaches not enough to dispel 'misogynistic' behaviour
World.content:
If you asked generative AI to create an image of a sports coach, it would likely serve up a middle-aged white man.

And while rooted in stereotypes, it would not necessarily be inaccurate.

The picture is slowly changing in some sports, although not substantial enough yet to disturb the algorithm.

The Australian Institute of Sport found the number of female head coaches in funded sports has nearly tripled since starting its Women in High Performance Coaching project in 2021.

The number now sits at more than 25 per cent, but AIS Director Matti Clements told ABC Sport that is still not good enough.

"Maybe we've had a history where we've just had male coaches coaching our best athletes," she said.

"We want to make sure the right people are coaching our athletes at the right time, female or male coaches."

AIS director Matti Clements says many female coaches still face key barriers. (ABC News: Peter Healy)

The AIS report found many women coaches have experienced bad behaviour, which was "in some cases appalling, misogynistic and abusive," as well as challenges managing careers alongside having a family, and difficulties even getting a foot in the door, let alone climbing the ladder.

It highlighted the need for leaders within the sporting sector to drive cultural change to address the barriers.

"As a system, we've had a real focus in the last couple of years of wellbeing being fundamental to high performance sport in this country," Clements said.

"If you look at wellbeing as a sustainable high-performance lever, that will encourage all different types of people to stay in our system, female coaches included.

"Perhaps historically, high-performance sport in this country has not been as welcoming for female coaches as it has been for male coaches."

Clements pointed out some of the strategies which have helped deliver positive results over the past four years include visibility of high profile coaches, having conversations at the highest levels, re-evaluating recruitment practices, and targeted development.

Sauvage leading the way

Louise Sauvage is one of Australia's most decorated Paralympians, and since retiring in 2004, has established herself as a leading coach in para wheelchair track and road racing.

She has noticed an evolution over the past 20 years.

Louise Sauvage has been an elite coach for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"It's been really good to see that infrastructure and also the investment into women's coaching," she told ABC Sport.

"Our athletes are almost 50-50 male, female, so to have that balance is perfect.

"And I think women bring something a little different to the male coaches as well. So I think it's important that we encourage them to continue on in those roles and to show the identity and what we can bring as female coaches."

Sauvage is also one of very few elite coaches with disability across the Australian sporting landscape, and acknowledged it has not always been an easy path for her.

"I think some of the barriers were definitely identifying what you could or couldn't do or how the workarounds would work," she said.

"And also talking with your national sporting organisation and how you can get past them or what help you might need and then you can just be as effective as any other coach.

"I think it's about communication more than anything and not just looking at something [and saying] 'oh, I can't do that.'

"[You should ask] how can you do it? How can we make it work for you so that you can progress as a coach?"

She added having coaches with shared lived experiences was a valuable asset for athletes.

"They already know that I know how they're feeling or what they need because I've been there and I've done that," she said.

"But things evolve all the time, so I need to keep learning as well. But I really do think a lot of the athletes do appreciate that the understanding is already there."

The professional picture

The AIS report focused on sports it funds, largely rooted in the Olympic and Paralympic arena, but many of the issues raised prevail in the professional codes too.

Four of the 18 of AFLW head coaches are women, one of 12 in the NRLW, one of 11 in the A-League Women and two of eight in the WBBL (last season).

The WNBL is close to parity with four of the nine coaches women, and as the country's number one female participation sport, five of Super Netball's eight coaches were female last season.

Like the dearth of disabled coaches, there are also very few First Nations, or culturally diverse head coaches, across men's and women's sports.

Clements said diversity in coaching simply makes sense.

"The sports are seeing the value of it in terms of performance outcomes. So this is not just a nice to have, we're doing it because it feels good," she said.

"It absolutely is a competitive advantage and that's what's going to engage our sports to continue to focus on this because we want to have the best games ever in Brisbane and in order to do that we have to make sure we've got the best people coaching."

World.title: Cats confirm Kolodjashnij unavailable to play amid concussion waiver saga
World.content:
The player at the centre of a concussion waiver controversy, Geelong's Jake Kolodjashnij, will not play this weekend as the club prepares to find out whether it will face sanctions.

It emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with a player, who had had a history of concussions.

Kolodjashnij went public confirming he was the player involved.

The waiver has since been removed from his contract.

"Geelong Cats defender Jake Kolodjashnij will be unavailable for selection at AFL or VFL level this weekend," the club said a statement late on Tuesday.

"The care and wellbeing of Jake remains the club's priority, and the club will continue to support him and his family through this period."

The Cats had until the end of Tuesday to respond to the "please explain" from the AFL over the concussion waiver that Kolodjashnij signed but which was never seen by the AFL or the AFLPA.

Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's please explain as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board had held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Media reports on Tuesday said that the AFL Commission had hired independent legal counsel to help determine whether the Cats should face sanctions over the issue.

The 31-year-old Kolodjashnij was drafted by the club in 2013 and he has played 209 games for Geelong.

He last played at AFL level for the Cats against GWS a month ago.

His twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, was forced to retire in 2020 due to concussion issues.

World.title: Veteran Manly prop Nathan Brown outlines NRL exit plan
World.content:
Manly prop Nathan Brown has revealed he decided at the start of the season this would be his last in the NRL, as the veteran forward eyes a move to the Super League.

Off contract at the end of 2026, Brown has confirmed he will finish up at Manly this year as the Sea Eagles begin a changing of the guard in the forward pack.

Brown's final month at Manly will take on even more importance on Friday night, after he was called in to start for the first time in two years against the Dolphins amid the Sea Eagles' forwards shortage.

The 33-year-old is still hoping to exit the NRL in a finals series, with Manly likely needing to win their last four games to return to the top eight.

Munster free to play Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster avoids suspension after the NRL match review committee downgrades his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

"I just knew it was my time to call it quits in the NRL … I made my debut in 2013, so it's my 14th year. When your time's up, your time is up," Brown told AAP.

"The last thing I wanted to do was sit on the fence with whether I want to stay or go overseas.

"It's just made everything a lot easier to go all in this year and enjoy every moment, every training session and every game."

Brown was regarded as one of the most aggressive forwards in the game when he debuted at Wests Tigers in 2013, as well as during a two-year stint at South Sydney.

Nathan Brown played six seasons at the Eels, making his Origin debut while at the club. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yeung)

He came into his own at Parramatta, playing two State of Origins for NSW in 2020 and the 2022 grand final for the Eels before reviving his career with a train-and-trial deal at Manly in 2024.

"I find it funny [looking back at old footage)]" said Brown, who is on track to reach 200 games this month.

"When I started, I was a lot bigger. I wasn't really that fit. I was a bit overweight for my size and my position. And I had a different attitude back then.

"But at the same time, you learn a lot from it. You feel grateful that you had to go through those things."

Brown's NRL retirement comes with fellow veteran Manly prop Siua Taukeiaho off contract after breaking his leg in two places in May.

The Sea Eagles have signed props Davvy Moale and Toni Mataele for next year, while Kayliss Fatialofa will arrive as a highly-heralded second rower.

Teenage prop Simi Laiafi has also shown promise starting this year alongside Taniela Paseka, and looms as a long-term prospect.

Brown said he was proud of the impact he was able to have off the bench this year, still hitting the line with gusto.

"You don't want to be finishing by just clutching at the straws and hanging on by a thread," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I feel like I can probably still physically play another year in the NRL. But in the mental side of things, I'm just ready."

Manly expect to be without prop Paseka for at least a fortnight after he injured his knee against Melbourne last week, in a seismic blow to their finals chances.

Ethan Bullemor (concussion) remains sidelined, while Kobe Hetherington (biceps) last week joined Taukeiaho in being out for the season.

Second-rower Ben Trbojevic (concussion) is also still out, while his superstar brother Tom has been kept on ice for another week in his return from a hamstring injury.

AAP

World.title: Inside Donald Trump's 'Hunger Games'-style athletics contest
World.content:
Anderson Reid, representing Puerto Rico, sprinted onto a military-style bootcamp course to the cheers of supporting families and friends.

Thrift Shop by Macklemore & Ryan Lewis played as he crawled, sprinted and carried jerry cans, vying to top the times of 119 other teenagers between the ages of 14 and 17 for a chance to win a university scholarship.

Anderson Reid says contestants did not have to currently live in the state or territory they represented, but did not clarify what ties he had to Puerto Rico. (Instagram: andersonreid88)

The Patriot Games 2026 were announced in December 2025 by US President Donald Trump, who billed it as "an unprecedented four-day athletic event featuring the greatest high school athletes".

"One young man and one young women from each state and territory, but I promise there will be no men playing in women's sports," he said.

From 50 states and a few more

One hundred and twenty competitors made it to Ohio to compete in the three-day-long athletic competition, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the United States.

The ABC has identified participants from Puerto Rico, Guam, the Shawnee Tribe and the US Virgin Islands, but not from American Samoa or other Native American groups.

However, there has been speculation some athletes might not live in the state or territory they represent.

Reid is representing Puerto Rico, but does not appear to live there, with one Instagram commenter asking, "Isn't he from Texas?".

Videos on Reid's YouTube channel show clips from Daikin Park stadium in Houston, Texas.

Responding to another comment on Instagram, Reid said "[Contestants] don't have to be currently living in the state or territory they are representing".

"They do have to have some sort of association with it such as living there or having social [family] ties to it," Reid said.

Little is known about the Freedom 250 Patriot Games selection committee, which chose the athletes based on video applications and personal essays. (AP: Nate Manley)

The idea behind the Patriot Games drew immediate comparison to The Hunger Games, a series of books by Suzanne Collins, which were later adapted into a multi-billion-dollar film franchise.

Patriot Games organisers Freedom250 said the event would "bring together outstanding young Americans from across the nation to compete, inspire, and showcase the values that have shaped the United States for nearly 250 years".

It's a unique qualification process, as unlike the Junior Olympics or national sports competitions, the pre-selection method did not involve qualifying rounds, but rather a video application process.

'I didn't think I'd get on'

Chris Brennan is representing North Carolina at the Patriot Games, and has been sharing each step of the experience on his social media.

In an interview with Trump-aligned influencer Adam Francisco Brennan said he stumbled across the Patriot Games online.

US President Donald Trump promoted the event as a showcase of the nation's best student athletes. (Supplied: X/Freedom250)

"I was just on Instagram one day, scrolling, scrolling and I saw an  and I was like, 'Hey, I heard Trump talking about that,'" Mr Brennan said.

"I clicked, submitted, I made a quick 5-minute video application.

"Honestly I think it was a little bit of luck and a little bit of my personality."

Chris Brennan posts conservative content on Instagram and, in an interview, said women couldn't compete with men athletically. (Instagram: notchris71)

Brennan then made it into the next round, and was asked to write an essay and answer "personal questions".

He later interviewed several of his fellow competitors in Baltimore, and they described stumbling on the Patriot Games like he did.

"I think it was on TikTok and I did it as a joke with my friend," Owen Carter of South Carolina said.

"I didn't think I'd get on."

The youth from North Carolina also runs a social media page called Club America, which features Christian content and Charlie Kirk quotes.

Some competitors said they prepared for the Patriot Games with cardio and pre-existing fitness routines.

Campbell Remus of Minnesota also participates in "Ninja Warrior" contests and other athletic competitions. (AP: Nate Manley)

Campbell Remus from Minnesota said she trains year round for track, cross country and the "Ninja Warrior" obstacle and fitness challenge, while Mr Carter said he went for "a lot of runs" despite not having much time to prepare.

On August 9 the athletes completed the presidential physical fitness test, a former national benchmark of core, upper body and cardio fitness retired in 2013. They also competed in team games of dodgeball and kick ball.

Joshua Chechile of Vermont participated in the 55-metre hurdles during day one of the Patriot Games, one of many different athletic events. (AP: Nate Manley)

The next day, competitors completed a multi-sport skill challenge called the varsity circuit, along with a military style bootcamp obstacle course.

The games will conclude at 7pm on August 11, local time, with semi-finals, finals and team competitions like tug of war.

'Follow my dreams without financial burden'

In her application video, incoming freshman Sophie Skidmore of West Virginia appeared with her neck adorned in sports medals.

"I'm always looking for my next challenge," she said.

"As for the scholarship it would help me follow my dreams without financial burden."

Skidmore was eliminated in day two of the qualifiers.

Trump commemorates America 250 The occasion was complicated by severe storms that gathered near Washington, forcing event organisers to order an earlier evacuation.

The top male and female athlete will each receive a $US125,000 university scholarship, but according to a report by the Education Data Initiative, the average cost of attending an out-of-state, public school in the US is more than $US182,000.

World.title: Slater still firing at 54 at Tahiti Pro, eliminating Medina
World.content:
Kelly Slater has advanced to the third round of the Tahiti Pro after the 54-year-old American overcame Brazil's Gabriel Medina and ​some heavy wipeouts at the 2024 Paris Olympics venue of Teahupo'o.

Slater's emotional Margaret River exit Surfing legend Kelly Slater holds back tears as his career effectively ends at Western Australia's Margaret River Pro, although the 11-time world champion is hoping for one last wildcard in Fiji.

Slater, who recently underwent hip surgery, retired from full-time competition in 2024 and welcomed a third child earlier this year ​but showed he had ‌lost none of his competitive edge against three-times world champion Medina.

In dangerous, challenging waves, Slater got smashed on his first attempt and was hit even harder on ‌his second wave, breaking his board in two.

But the Floridian recovered ⁠and threaded a long, deep tube that scored a 9.73 ‌out of 10 to take ​the lead.

He ‌then backed it up with another excellent score to advance over Medina, who beat Slater in an epic final at the same venue in 2014.

"I don't know if I'll ever have another heat with him, and ​he ‌got me last time," said Slater, who dominated the first day of competition.

He said he had been motivated by criticism of the ⁠decision to award him a wildcard ‌to compete.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"You see those comments, ‌a lot of people doubting me or saying [the opportunity] should have gone to ‌a local wildcard," he said. "Even after all this time, I have something to prove."

Slater finished with an excellent two-wave ‌total ​of 19.06 out of ⁠20 to set up a third-round meeting with reigning champion Jack Robinson of Australia, who was pushed hard by countryman Callum Robson in round two.

California's Griffin Colapinto, who was born six years after ⁠Slater won the first of his 11 world titles, was the only man to better Slater's ‌performance in ‌the second round, racking up a perfect 10-point ride ​on his way to a season-high heat total of 19.6 out of 20.

Tech.title: Xbox Elite 3 prototype pad leaks with tiny built-in screen
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Did a prototype Microsoft gamepad fall off the back of a truck? We can’t say, but a Redditor has legit-looking photos of a prototype Xbox controller that’s almost certainly the Xbox Elite Series 3. Incredibly, they claim they bought the pad for $200 on OfferUp.

In May, a Brazilian regulator’s leaked images revealed that Xbox Elite 3 would have new two new scroll wheels on the bottom edge, a second wireless mode to connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming servers, and a new “Pair Button” that can also switch between those servers and your console.

Where might that pair button live? Today, we have a possible answer: it might sit right next to the Xbox Elite 3’s built-in screen, a previously unrevealed feature.

The screen looks almost exactly like the leaked diagram from May showing the mode switch dialogue, with a pair button at the left:

The Anatel image from May, overlaid atop the new prototype controller photos. Image: u/ssuberlex (Reddit)

And if I’m not mistaken, the screen on Redditor ssuberlex’s controller is displaying the little XCloud rocket ship next to an Xbox Series X.

The screen can apparently display other things, too. In another photo, it shows a URL that takes me to a Microsoft cloud resource I don’t have permission to view. That lends these images some extra credibility. Unfortunately, the Redditor says the controller doesn’t work. “It does not pair with an Xbox nor with a cable. Just the red light blinking but doesn’t do any thing wired or wireless,” they wrote.

In other photos, we can see the controller’s new scroll wheels, its four rear paddles, its battery compartment, its carrying case, and a different detachable D-pad design than we saw in the May leak. The Redditor says the triggers are clicky when you lock them to the hair-trigger position.

Previous Next









1 / 6 Image: u/ssuberlex (Reddit)

But beyond the screen, the most intriguing image is from inside the controller’s battery compartment. It appears Microsoft has made efforts to make this controller home repairable by including a QR code that presumably leads to a repair website, and accessible Torx T6 screws.

Still, none of these features are for certain. The controller is clearly a prototype, with “NOT FOR SALE” labels on both the pad and its removable 5.8 watt-hour battery, and many placeholder ID numbers for various regulatory bodies.

Tom Warren, The Verge’s Microsoft expert, says his sources believe this controller is still coming later this year.

Tech.title: An FCC filing points to new Sonos headphones coming soon
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

In addition to the S52A designation, one of the submitted documents shows an oval diagram — likely the ear cup — marked with the name Sonos Ace Ultra, although that name isn’t listed anywhere else. It follows the naming scheme Sonos has used in the past with its Arc and Arc Ultra soundbars. The documents also list color options we’ll likely see, which extend beyond the white and black of the Ace. The five colors named are “greige,” shadow black, agave, blush, and sand.

There’s also indication of testing for local networks over 2.4 and 5GHz bands. This could be just for the same TV swapping capability we saw on the Sonos Ace, or it could mean that these new headphones will support music streaming over Wi-Fi like Sonos’ speakers.

It’s been over two years since the Sonos Ace headphones were released, and that launch was overshadowed by the troublesome redesigned app rollout, which was likely pushed out early because the old app would not have supported the Ace. While the Sonos Ace were comfortable and stylish with good sound and ANC, they weren’t quite as good as comparatively priced headphones of the time like the Sony WH-1000XM5 or Sennheiser Momentum 4. And because of the app issues, the Sonos ecosystem integration was buggy.

But Sonos has come a long way and recovered from those woeful app relaunch days with some strong product releases, including the Arc Ultra soundbar and Play speaker. If Sonos takes the lessons learned from the original Ace — and we do indeed see new headphones in the coming weeks or months — they could signal the full return of Sonos.

Tech.title: ChatGPT and Gemini both just passed 1 billion users
Tech.content:
For the 14th time, a Google product has hit 1 billion users. Google CEO Sundar Pichai posted on X that a billion people are using Gemini every month, and that Gemini is Google’s fastest-growing product ever.

A billion users is a huge milestone, but Google isn’t the first AI app to hit it. OpenAI’s ChatGPT hit the mark a few weeks ago, though the company buried the announcement that “more than 1 billion people are putting ChatGPT to work” in an otherwise anodyne blog post about how people use AI. External data suggested ChatGPT crossed 1 billion users as early as this June, but OpenAI hadn’t announced anything until that post on August 6th. OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says ChatGPT crossed 1 billion monthly users some time ago, and hit a billion a week in July.

The metrics, and the growth they represent, are somewhat complicated here. OpenAI said that ChatGPT had 900 million weekly active users in February of this year, and reaching 1 billion five months later represents a significant slowdown in growth for ChatGPT, which was for years touted as the fastest-growing software ever. McCallum declined to say how many monthly users ChatGPT has.

Google, meanwhile, announced in February that Gemini had 750 million monthly users, before reporting 950 million in late July on its earnings call, and Google spokesperson Alex Joseph says it reached 1 billion last week before announcing it today. (Claude appears to be growing fast, but Anthropic doesn’t disclose its user data, and estimates put its user numbers in the tens of millions.) There’s no easy way to compare weekly and monthly users, of course, but the simplest read is that ChatGPT is the larger of the platforms but Gemini may be the faster growing.

These Google numbers, by the way, all appear to refer directly to the Gemini app itself, which would mean all the places Google has shoved Gemini into its other products don’t count. The Gemini that comes preinstalled on Android phones seemingly does, though, which is a huge win for Google — Gemini chief Josh Woodward posted that Gemini has more than 100 million active users on iOS, which would mean by extension that the vast majority of Gemini users are also Android users. You can see why OpenAI is so interested in building its own hardware.

The AI race in general has tightened significantly this year. Anthropic’s Claude Code became a phenomenon and forced OpenAI to catch up with Codex, while Google began integrating Gemini into seemingly every surface of its products. The companies’ models have consistently leapfrogged each other, and they’re all suddenly in a race with models coming out of China. But for a long time, ChatGPT was the de facto brand for AI chatbots, and while it’s still seemingly the most popular and well known of its kind, its once commanding lead appears to have largely evaporated. The race to a billion users is over — now these companies have to race to find things for those users to do, and ways to make money in the process.

Tech.title: Threads has a VR app now
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta has launched a Threads app for Meta Quest VR headsets, the company announced on Tuesday. The launch follows Meta bringing the app to its Ray-Ban Display AR glasses last month and the recent news that the platform has crossed 500 million monthly active users.

It seems like a pretty full-featured app. Meta says that with the Threads VR app, you can do things like browse feeds, make posts, like and reply to posts, visit profiles, search, and watch videos — you know, Threads stuff.

“We designed the new Threads app for Meta Quest to make using VR more social than ever,” Meta says. “Whether you want to keep up with conversations during a game, riff on the latest TV show or hit album with friends, or simply do fast check-ins between daily tasks, Threads can enhance your VR experience with a dedicated native app.”

You can download the app from Meta’s store.

Tech.title: Google’s free streaming service now lets you pick shows and movies to watch
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google TV Freeplay, the company’s free, ad-supported streaming service, now supports video on demand. Instead of tuning into Google TV Freeplay’s selection of always-on channels, you can now choose from over 10,000 shows and movies to watch whenever you want.

The update introduces titles like Lady Bird, Seventeen Again, and Hell’s Kitchen, according to Google’s announcement. The company has also expanded its live TV lineup to include more than 300 channels dedicated to news, sports, reality TV, true crime, and more. Some of these new channels include World of Love Island, Yahoo! Sports Network, Bloomberg TV Plus, and The Martha Stewart Channel.

Image: Google

Free and ultra-cheap streaming is on the rise as major streamers continue to raise their prices. Google TV Freeplay joins Tubi, The Roku Channel, and Pluto TV in offering free, ad-supported content on demand, while Disney Plus is considering launching a free streaming tier as well.

Google says it plans to continue updating its Freeplay library throughout the year.

Tech.title: Another OpenAI executive takes off
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Brad Lightcap, OpenAI’s special projects lead and the company’s former COO, announced his departure after an eight-year stint at the AI lab. In an internal memo he later posted to X, Lightcap told colleagues he’d be starting “something new.”

“Over the last few months, I’ve been focused on the next horizon and what would stand in the way of mission success,” Lightcap wrote. “I believe there are a few important new things the world will need to get right as we enter this next period. I … am excited to help you all advance the mission from a different vantage point.” He added that he’d still be around for the next few weeks.

Lightcap’s role has changed a lot over the past year and a half. In March 2025, his role as COO expanded to include overseeing OpenAI’s “business and day-to-day operations,” heading up global deployment and “focusing on business strategy, key partnerships, infrastructure, and operational excellence to maximize the impact of our research.” Then in January 2026, Lightcap took a step back from leading the company’s enterprise push as far as product and engineering but stayed in charge of commercial functions. (Embattled AI executive Barret Zoph took over enterprise before departing about five months later.) In April, Lightcap officially stepped down from his COO role, transitioning into a new one leading the team’s “special projects” and reporting to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Denise Dresser, the company’s CRO, took over a significant portion of his former role.

It’s not the only high-profile departure from OpenAI’s executive team in recent months: OpenAI’s AGI chief, Fidji Simo, officially departed her role in July after a stint on medical leave, and in April, CMO Kate Rouch also stepped down for health reasons. There’s also been a significant amount of company reorganizing and C-suite changes, with company president Greg Brockman taking control of the product side of things, and the company vowing to cut out “side quests” in favor of key revenue drivers as it prepares to go public over the coming year.

“It always amazes me how quickly the world has adopted our tools and rallied behind our mission,” Lightcap wrote. “I hope we will continue to earn their trust.”
